name: Neon Tetra
description: The neon tetra is a small, brilliantly colored freshwater fish native to the blackwater streams of the Amazon basin in South America. Its signature electric-blue stripe runs horizontally from the nose to the adipose fin, with a vivid red stripe extending from the mid-body to the tail. In the wild, these fish inhabit soft, acidic waters shaded by dense rainforest canopy. Their iridescent coloring evolved to help them stay visible to schoolmates in the dark, tannin-stained waters. Neon tetras are one of the most popular aquarium fish worldwide, prized for their peaceful nature and the stunning visual effect of a large school shimmering under aquarium lights.
care_tips: Keep neon tetras in groups of at least eight to reduce stress and encourage natural schooling behavior. They thrive in a well-planted tank with subdued lighting and a dark substrate, which brings out their best coloring. Avoid housing them with large or aggressive species that may view them as food. Neon tetras are sensitive to sudden water parameter changes, so perform small, frequent water changes rather than large infrequent ones. They are susceptible to neon tetra disease, a parasitic condition with no cure, so always quarantine new fish before adding them to an established school.

name: Betta Fish
description: The betta, also known as the Siamese fighting fish, originates from the shallow rice paddies, floodplains, and slow-moving streams of Thailand, Cambodia, and Vietnam. Males are famous for their elaborate finnage and intense coloring, which have been selectively bred over centuries into dozens of tail types including halfmoon, crowntail, and plakat. Bettas possess a labyrinth organ that allows them to breathe atmospheric air, an adaptation to their oxygen-poor natural habitats. Males are highly territorial and will flare their gill covers and fins as a threat display toward rivals. Despite their aggressive reputation toward other males, bettas can be surprisingly personable and often learn to recognize their keepers.
care_tips: Despite common misconceptions, bettas need at least a 5-gallon heated and filtered tank to thrive. Keep the water temperature stable between 76-82°F and maintain a gentle filter flow, as strong currents stress their long fins. Never house two males together, and be cautious with female bettas as well unless you have experience with sorority setups. Provide floating plants or broad leaves near the surface where bettas like to rest. Feed a varied diet of quality betta pellets supplemented with frozen bloodworms or brine shrimp. Watch for fin rot, which often results from poor water quality or temperature drops.

name: Guppy
description: Guppies are small, vibrantly colored livebearers originally from the rivers and ponds of Trinidad, Barbados, and northeastern South America. Males display an extraordinary range of color patterns and tail shapes, from solid reds and blues to multicolored mosaic patterns, making them one of the most genetically diverse ornamental fish. Females are larger and less colorful but can store sperm for months, producing multiple broods from a single mating. Guppies were historically introduced to tropical waterways worldwide as mosquito control agents. They are exceptionally hardy and adaptable, tolerating a wide range of water conditions, which makes them an ideal choice for beginner aquarists.
care_tips: Guppies breed prolifically, so keep an all-male group if you want to avoid population explosions, or provide dense floating plants like hornwort for fry to hide in. They prefer slightly hard, alkaline water and do well at a pH of 7.0-8.0. Feed a high-quality flake food supplemented with occasional frozen or live foods for the best color. Males may harass females relentlessly, so maintain a ratio of at least two females per male if keeping mixed groups. Watch for common ailments like ich and fin nipping, especially in overstocked tanks. Weekly 25% water changes keep them healthy and vibrant.

name: Corydoras Catfish
description: Corydoras catfish are small, armored bottom-dwellers native to the streams and rivers of South America, where they forage in groups along sandy or muddy substrates. Their bodies are covered in bony plates called scutes rather than typical scales, giving them a distinctive armored appearance. Corydoras are social fish that communicate through body language and even produce sounds by moving their pectoral spines. With over 170 described species and many more awaiting classification, they are one of the most species-rich genera of freshwater fish. Their endearing habit of winking, which is actually a rapid eye movement to aid feeding, and their constant bustling activity make them a favorite among aquarists.
care_tips: Always keep corydoras in groups of at least six, as they are highly social and become stressed or inactive when kept alone. Use smooth sand or fine gravel as substrate, since sharp gravel can damage their delicate barbels, leading to infections. They appreciate a moderate current and well-oxygenated water. Feed sinking pellets, wafers, and frozen foods like bloodworms, and make sure food actually reaches the bottom before other fish eat it all. Corydoras are sensitive to salt and many medications, so research treatments carefully before dosing. They occasionally dart to the surface to gulp air, which is normal behavior.

name: Angelfish
description: Freshwater angelfish are elegant cichlids native to the Amazon River basin, where they inhabit slow-moving, heavily vegetated waters among submerged tree roots and overhanging vegetation. Their tall, laterally compressed bodies and long, flowing fins allow them to navigate gracefully through dense aquatic plants. Wild angelfish display silver bodies with dark vertical bars that serve as camouflage, while captive breeding has produced varieties including marble, koi, black, and platinum. Angelfish are intelligent and can recognize their owners, often swimming to the front of the tank at feeding time. They form monogamous breeding pairs and both parents actively guard their eggs and fry.
care_tips: Angelfish need a tall tank of at least 30 gallons due to their vertical body shape, with a minimum height of 18 inches. Keep them in groups of five or more when young to allow natural pair formation, but be prepared to separate aggressive pairs during breeding. Avoid housing them with small fish like neon tetras, which adult angelfish may eat. They prefer soft, slightly acidic water with temperatures around 78-82°F. Provide tall plants like Amazon swords and vertical driftwood for them to feel secure. Feed a varied diet of quality flakes, pellets, and frozen foods. Watch for hexamita, a parasitic disease that causes hole-in-the-head symptoms.

name: Platy
description: Platies are cheerful, easy-going livebearers originally from the coastal streams of Central America, primarily Mexico, Guatemala, and Honduras. Through extensive selective breeding, they now come in a dazzling array of colors and patterns including red wag, sunset, Mickey Mouse, blue, and tuxedo varieties. Like other livebearers, females give birth to fully formed, free-swimming fry rather than laying eggs. Platies are active mid-level swimmers that spend their days exploring every corner of the aquarium. Their hardy constitution, peaceful temperament, and willingness to eat almost anything make them one of the best starter fish for new aquarium hobbyists.
care_tips: Platies are undemanding but prefer moderately hard, slightly alkaline water with a pH of 7.0-8.2. Keep them in groups with more females than males to prevent harassment. They are enthusiastic eaters that readily accept flakes, pellets, and frozen foods, but benefit from occasional vegetable matter like blanched zucchini or spirulina-based foods. Platies breed easily and frequently, so plan for fry or keep single-sex groups. Maintain the tank at 70-78°F and perform regular water changes to prevent common issues like fin rot and ich. They mix well with other peaceful community fish of similar size.

name: Molly
description: Mollies are versatile livebearers found naturally in freshwater and brackish coastal habitats from the southern United States through Mexico and Central America. The most popular varieties include the black molly, dalmatian molly, gold dust molly, and the impressive sailfin molly with its large dorsal fin. Mollies are unique among common aquarium fish in their ability to adapt to a wide range of salinities, from pure freshwater to full marine conditions. They are active, social fish that establish loose hierarchies within their groups. Males are easily identified by their gonopodium, a modified anal fin used for reproduction, and they spend much of their time displaying to females.
care_tips: Mollies thrive in hard, alkaline water and many keepers find that adding a small amount of aquarium salt improves their health and reduces susceptibility to disease. Keep them at 75-82°F in a tank of at least 20 gallons, as they are active swimmers that need room. Maintain a higher ratio of females to males to reduce stress from constant male attention. Mollies are prone to a condition called molly disease or shimmies, characterized by a rocking, shimmying motion, which is usually caused by poor water quality or inappropriate parameters. Feed a varied diet with plenty of plant-based foods, as they are natural algae grazers. They breed readily, and females can produce 40-100 fry every 4-6 weeks.

name: Cherry Barb
description: The cherry barb is a small, brightly colored freshwater fish endemic to the shaded streams and rivers of Sri Lanka's wet zone rainforests. Males develop an intense cherry-red coloration during breeding season, while females remain a more subdued pinkish-brown with a distinctive dark lateral stripe. In the wild, cherry barbs are listed as vulnerable due to habitat loss from deforestation and collection for the aquarium trade, though virtually all specimens sold today are captive-bred. Unlike some other barb species, cherry barbs are genuinely peaceful and make excellent community tank residents. They are active foragers that spend their time picking at plants and substrate for small invertebrates and algae.
care_tips: Keep cherry barbs in groups of at least six, with a mix of males and females for the best color displays. Males will intensify their red coloring when competing for female attention. Provide a well-planted tank with areas of shade, as they naturally inhabit forest streams. They prefer slightly soft, acidic to neutral water at 73-81°F. Feed high-quality flakes and small pellets supplemented with frozen daphnia and brine shrimp. Cherry barbs are generally hardy and disease-resistant, making them an excellent choice for planted community tanks. They will eat some soft algae and can help control minor algae issues.

name: Zebra Danio
description: The zebra danio is a small, energetic freshwater fish native to the streams and rice paddies of South Asia, particularly India, Bangladesh, and Nepal. Its distinctive horizontal blue and silver stripes run the full length of its body, giving it its common name. Zebra danios were the first vertebrate to be cloned and are widely used in scientific research, including the development of the fluorescent GloFish varieties. These fish are incredibly active, spending most of their time darting rapidly around the upper levels of the tank. Their hardiness is legendary in the hobby, as they tolerate temperatures from the low 60s to the mid-80s Fahrenheit and adapt to virtually any water chemistry.
care_tips: Zebra danios are extremely active swimmers that need a tank with plenty of horizontal swimming space, ideally at least 20 gallons long. Keep them in schools of at least six, as solitary danios can become stressed and nippy. They prefer cooler water around 65-77°F and do not actually need a heater in most room-temperature homes. Provide a tight-fitting lid, as they are accomplished jumpers. Feed a staple of quality flake food with occasional frozen or live foods for variety. Zebra danios make excellent dither fish for timid species and are often recommended for cycling new tanks due to their resilience, though fishless cycling is always the more humane approach.

name: Dwarf Gourami
description: The dwarf gourami is a strikingly beautiful labyrinth fish native to the slow-moving, heavily vegetated waters of India, Bangladesh, and Pakistan. Males display brilliant alternating stripes of iridescent blue and flame-red, while females are a more modest silvery color. Popular color variants include powder blue, flame red, and neon blue. Like bettas, dwarf gouramis possess a labyrinth organ that allows them to breathe air directly from the surface, an adaptation to warm, oxygen-depleted waters. Males build elaborate bubble nests at the water's surface using air bubbles coated in saliva, where they tend their eggs with remarkable dedication.
care_tips: Provide a calm, well-planted tank with floating plants and minimal surface agitation to allow comfortable air breathing and bubble nest construction. Dwarf gouramis are prone to iridovirus (DGIV), a serious and often fatal viral disease common in mass-produced fish. Buy from reputable breeders and quarantine new specimens for at least two weeks. Keep only one male per tank unless the aquarium is very large with broken sight lines, as males can be territorial. They prefer soft, slightly acidic water at 77-82°F. Feed a varied diet including quality flakes, frozen bloodworms, and small live foods. Avoid boisterous tankmates like tiger barbs that may nip their threadlike pelvic fins.

name: Bristlenose Pleco
description: The bristlenose pleco is a compact, hardworking catfish from the rivers and streams of South America, particularly the Amazon and Orinoco basins. Males develop distinctive fleshy tentacles on their snouts as they mature, which are used to attract females and may mimic the appearance of food-carrying fry. Unlike the common pleco, bristlenose plecos stay relatively small at around 4-5 inches, making them suitable for moderately sized community tanks. They are primarily nocturnal, spending daylight hours wedged into caves and crevices before emerging at night to methodically graze every surface in the tank. Bristlenose plecos are among the most effective algae-eating fish available to hobbyists.
care_tips: While bristlenose plecos are excellent algae eaters, they cannot survive on algae alone and need supplemental feeding with sinking algae wafers, blanched vegetables like zucchini and cucumber, and occasional protein foods. Provide plenty of driftwood, as they rasp on it for essential fiber and nutrients. Each pleco needs at least one cave or hiding spot, and caves are essential for breeding. They produce a surprising amount of waste for their size, so maintain strong filtration and regular water changes. Keep the water well-oxygenated with moderate flow at 73-81°F. Males can be territorial over caves, so provide more hiding spots than you have plecos.

name: Cardinal Tetra
description: The cardinal tetra is a jewel-like freshwater fish from the blackwater tributaries of the Rio Negro and Orinoco basins in South America. Often confused with the neon tetra, the cardinal is distinguished by its red stripe extending the full length of its body, from head to tail, rather than just the posterior half. In the wild, cardinal tetras inhabit extremely soft, acidic waters stained dark brown by tannins from decomposing leaves. They are one of the most commercially important ornamental fish species, with millions exported from Brazil and Colombia annually. A large school of cardinal tetras in a darkwater aquarium setup is widely considered one of the most spectacular displays in the freshwater hobby.
care_tips: Cardinal tetras are more sensitive to water conditions than their neon tetra cousins and do best in soft, acidic water with a pH of 5.0-7.0. Add Indian almond leaves or alder cones to provide beneficial tannins that mimic their natural habitat and have antifungal properties. Keep them in schools of at least ten for the most natural behavior and stunning visual impact. They prefer dim lighting and a dark substrate, which showcases their iridescent colors beautifully. Avoid keeping them with large or aggressive fish. Feed a varied diet of quality micro-pellets, crushed flakes, and frozen foods like daphnia and baby brine shrimp.

name: Harlequin Rasbora
description: The harlequin rasbora is a graceful, copper-toned schooling fish native to the peat swamp forests and blackwater streams of Malaysia, Singapore, Sumatra, and Thailand. Its most distinctive feature is the dark, triangular or lamb-chop-shaped patch on the rear half of its body, set against a warm pinkish-copper background. Harlequin rasboras are true schooling fish that swim in tight, coordinated formations, creating a mesmerizing display of synchronized movement. They are among the most popular and widely available rasbora species in the aquarium trade. In the wild, they spawn by depositing eggs on the undersides of broad leaves, a behavior they will replicate in the aquarium with plants like cryptocorynes.
care_tips: Keep harlequin rasboras in groups of at least eight, as they are most confident and active in larger schools. They prefer soft, slightly acidic water at 73-82°F with subdued lighting and plenty of plants. A dark substrate and tannin-stained water bring out the richest coloring. These rasboras are peaceful and make ideal companions for other gentle community fish, dwarf shrimp, and small corydoras. Feed quality micro-pellets and flakes supplemented with frozen daphnia and brine shrimp. They are generally hardy once established but can be sensitive during initial acclimation, so drip-acclimate new fish slowly over at least an hour.

name: German Blue Ram
description: The German blue ram is a small, spectacularly colored dwarf cichlid native to the Orinoco River basin in Venezuela and Colombia. Its body shimmers with iridescent blue spangles over a golden-yellow base, accented by a prominent black spot on the flank and vivid red eyes. The German blue ram is the result of selective breeding from the wild ram cichlid, emphasizing blue coloration and compact body shape. Unlike many cichlids, rams are relatively peaceful and can be kept in community tanks with appropriately sized tankmates. Breeding pairs form strong bonds and both parents share egg-guarding duties, fanning the eggs and defending their territory from intruders.
care_tips: German blue rams are among the more demanding community fish and require warm, soft, acidic water at 82-86°F with a pH below 7.0. They are very sensitive to nitrates, so keep levels below 20 ppm with frequent water changes and avoid overstocking. Provide sandy substrate for their natural sifting behavior, along with flat rocks and broad leaves for potential spawning sites. They do best in a mature, well-cycled tank and should not be added to newly set up aquariums. Feed high-quality pellets, frozen bloodworms, and brine shrimp. Commercially bred rams are often treated with hormones to enhance color, which can shorten their lifespan, so seek out reputable breeders.

name: Kuhli Loach
description: The kuhli loach is an eel-like bottom-dweller native to the slow-moving streams and forest floors of Southeast Asia, including Indonesia, Malaysia, and Thailand. Its slender, snake-like body features alternating bands of dark brown and pinkish-orange, giving it a distinctive and somewhat exotic appearance. Kuhli loaches are primarily nocturnal and spend daylight hours burrowed into substrate or hidden among roots and plant debris. They have tiny, downward-facing mouths equipped with sensitive barbels used to probe the substrate for food particles. Despite their shy nature, kuhli loaches become more active and visible when kept in groups, often piling together in communal hiding spots.
care_tips: Keep kuhli loaches in groups of at least six, as solitary individuals will hide permanently and you will rarely see them. Use fine sand substrate, as they love to burrow and sharp gravel can injure their scaleless skin. Provide plenty of hiding places using driftwood, caves, dense plants, and leaf litter. Cover filter intakes with fine sponge or mesh, as these slender fish can easily get sucked in. They prefer warm water at 75-86°F with a slightly acidic pH. Feed sinking foods after lights out, such as sinking pellets, frozen bloodworms, and live blackworms. Kuhli loaches are sensitive to medications, particularly those containing copper.

name: Black Skirt Tetra
description: The black skirt tetra, also known as the black widow tetra, is a hardy and distinctive fish from the Paraguay and Guapore river basins in South America. Its most striking feature is its large, flowing anal fin that creates a dramatic skirt-like silhouette, paired with two prominent vertical bars on its forward body. Young fish display the deepest black coloring, which gradually fades to a dark gray as they age. Black skirt tetras are active, confident mid-water swimmers that bring movement and personality to community aquariums. They are also the base species for the popular GloFish tetras, which are genetically modified to express fluorescent proteins.
care_tips: Black skirt tetras are one of the hardiest tetra species and tolerate a wide range of conditions, making them excellent for beginners. Keep them in schools of at least six to minimize any fin-nipping tendencies. Avoid housing them with long-finned or slow-moving fish like bettas or fancy guppies, as they may nip trailing fins. They prefer slightly soft, acidic to neutral water at 70-79°F. A spacious tank with open swimming areas and some planted sections provides the ideal environment. Feed quality flake food as a staple, supplemented with frozen or live foods. They can live 5-7 years with proper care.

name: Rummy Nose Tetra
description: The rummy-nose tetra is a sleek, torpedo-shaped schooling fish from the blackwater rivers of the Amazon basin. It is instantly recognizable by its brilliant red nose and face, which extends from the mouth to just behind the gill cover, contrasted with a distinctly striped black-and-white tail. The intensity of the red nose coloring serves as a reliable indicator of water quality and fish health, fading noticeably when conditions deteriorate. Rummy-nose tetras are considered one of the tightest schooling fish in the hobby, swimming in remarkably synchronized formations that rival marine species. This makes them a top choice for aquascaping enthusiasts seeking dramatic schooling effects.
care_tips: Rummy-nose tetras need stable, clean water with low nitrates to maintain their vivid red nose coloring. Keep them in groups of at least ten for the best schooling behavior in soft, slightly acidic water at 75-82°F. They are more sensitive to water quality than many tetras, so perform consistent weekly water changes and avoid adding them to uncycled tanks. Their red nose serves as a living water quality test: if it fades, check your parameters immediately. Provide moderate flow and open swimming areas along with planted sections for security. Feed varied foods including quality flakes, micro-pellets, and frozen daphnia.

name: Emperor Tetra
description: The emperor tetra is a regal-looking fish native to the Atrato and San Juan river basins in Colombia. Males develop stunning purple-blue bodies with a bold dark stripe running from nose to tail, accented by iridescent scales and elongated dorsal and caudal fin rays that create a crown-like appearance. Females are less colorful but display an attractive olive-brown tone with the same dark lateral stripe. Emperor tetras are peaceful, mid-water schooling fish that move with a calm, deliberate swimming style quite different from the frantic darting of many smaller tetras. Their subtle elegance and manageable size make them a sophisticated addition to planted community aquariums.
care_tips: Keep emperor tetras in groups of at least six, ideally with more females than males to spread out male attention. They prefer soft, slightly acidic water at 73-81°F with subdued lighting that highlights their iridescent coloring. A dark substrate and planted background make their colors pop. Emperor tetras are generally peaceful but males may spar mildly for dominance, displaying their extended fins without causing harm. Feed a varied diet of quality flakes, micro-pellets, and frozen foods. They thrive in mature, stable tanks and appreciate the addition of tannins from driftwood or Indian almond leaves.

name: Congo Tetra
description: The Congo tetra is a large, magnificently colored schooling fish from the Congo River basin in central Africa. Males are among the most beautiful freshwater fish, with shimmering scales that shift through shades of blue, gold, orange, and green depending on the light angle, complemented by flowing, elongated fin extensions. Females are more subdued in coloring but still attractive with golden-olive tones. Congo tetras are peaceful giants of the tetra world, reaching up to 3.5 inches, and their large, reflective scales create a spectacular light show when a school catches the aquarium lights. They are naturally found in murky, slow-moving tributaries with sandy bottoms and overhanging vegetation.
care_tips: Congo tetras need a spacious tank of at least 40 gallons to accommodate their active swimming and large school size. Keep them in groups of at least eight, with more females than males to reduce fin-nipping among rival males. They are timid fish that scare easily, so avoid sudden lighting changes and provide cover with floating plants. Congo tetras prefer slightly acidic to neutral water at 75-82°F with moderate flow. They are sensitive to poor water quality, so maintain regular water changes. Feed quality flake food and frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp to enhance their spectacular coloring.

name: Serpae Tetra
description: The serpae tetra is a fiery-red freshwater fish from the Amazon basin, found in the slow-moving backwaters and floodplain pools of Brazil, Argentina, and Paraguay. Its deep red-orange body is accented by a prominent black comma-shaped spot just behind the gill cover and dark edging on its fins. Serpae tetras are active, bold fish with a reputation for being more nippy than many other tetra species, especially when kept in too-small groups. In adequate numbers, they form a stunning school of constant red motion. Their hardiness and vivid coloring have made them a staple in the hobby for decades, though their semi-aggressive nature requires thoughtful tankmate selection.
care_tips: Keep serpae tetras in groups of at least eight or more to contain their nippy behavior within the school rather than directing it at other species. Avoid housing them with slow-moving, long-finned fish like bettas, angelfish, or fancy guppies. They prefer slightly soft, acidic water at 72-79°F and adapt well to a range of conditions. Provide a mix of open swimming space and planted areas. Feed a staple of quality flakes supplemented with frozen bloodworms and brine shrimp to maintain their deep red coloring. Their nippy tendencies decrease significantly in larger groups with ample space.

name: Glowlight Tetra
description: The glowlight tetra is a subtle, elegant fish from the Essequibo River in Guyana. Its translucent, peach-tinted body features a single iridescent orange-red stripe that runs from nose to tail, appearing to glow under aquarium lighting, particularly in dimly lit tanks. The effect is reminiscent of a glowing filament, which gives the species its common name. Glowlight tetras are among the most peaceful and unassuming of all tetra species, making them perfect companions for other gentle fish and shrimp. They are a classic choice for small, peaceful community setups and planted tanks where their warm, luminous stripe adds a touch of living light.
care_tips: Keep glowlight tetras in schools of at least six in soft, slightly acidic water at 74-82°F. They are at their most beautiful under subdued lighting with a dark substrate and background, which makes their glowing stripe appear even more vivid. Pair them with other small, peaceful species like other tetras, rasboras, and corydoras. They accept all standard aquarium foods readily, including flakes, micro-pellets, and frozen foods. Glowlight tetras are hardy and undemanding once established, though like most tetras they are sensitive to ammonia and nitrite spikes. A well-maintained, mature tank brings out the best in these understated gems.

name: Diamond Tetra
description: The diamond tetra is a shimmering gem of the freshwater world, native to Lake Valencia and its surrounding waters in Venezuela. Its scales are covered in a reflective, diamond-like sparkle that flashes brilliantly under light, particularly as the fish matures. Males develop impressively elongated dorsal fins that they display proudly during courtship and territorial disputes. The body has a warm, golden-olive base color that serves as the perfect canvas for its sparkling scales. Diamond tetras are peaceful, mid-water schooling fish that bring a touch of understated luxury to community aquariums. Unfortunately, they are increasingly rare in their native habitat due to pollution and habitat degradation.
care_tips: Keep diamond tetras in groups of at least six in a tank of 20 gallons or more. They prefer soft to moderately hard water at 75-82°F with good filtration and regular water changes. Their sparkling coloring intensifies with age and under the right conditions, so be patient with young specimens. Provide a mix of open swimming areas and planted sections. Males may display and spar gently but rarely cause harm. Feed quality flakes and pellets supplemented with frozen and live foods for the best growth and color development. They are generally hardy and adapt well to a range of conditions.

name: Flame Tetra
description: The flame tetra, also known as the Von Rio tetra, is a warm-toned fish originally from the coastal rivers near Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Its body displays a gradient of silver-olive near the head transitioning to fiery orange-red toward the tail, with two distinctive dark vertical bars behind the gill cover. Males develop more intense red coloring, especially during breeding displays. Flame tetras are peaceful, undemanding schooling fish that have been a staple in the aquarium hobby since the early 1900s. Though less flashy than some newer species, their warm, sunset-like coloring and easygoing nature make them a reliable choice for community tanks.
care_tips: Flame tetras are among the hardiest and most forgiving tetras, tolerating temperatures from 64-82°F and a range of water chemistries. Keep them in schools of six or more for natural behavior and the best color displays. They do well in both heated tropical setups and room-temperature tanks. Provide a planted tank with open swimming areas and subdued lighting to bring out their warmest colors. Feed standard flake food with occasional frozen or live food treats. They are generally disease-resistant and long-lived, making them an excellent choice for beginners who want an attractive, low-maintenance schooling fish.

name: Black Phantom Tetra
description: The black phantom tetra is a sophisticated-looking fish from the upper Paraguay and Guapore river basins in Brazil and Bolivia. Males are smoky gray-black with dramatically tall dorsal and anal fins that they spread wide during territorial displays, creating an impressive phantom-like silhouette. Females contrast beautifully with reddish-brown bodies and red-tinted fins. Males frequently engage in ritualized sparring displays, circling each other with fins fully extended in a dance-like confrontation that rarely results in any actual contact. This species is a refined alternative to more common tetras, offering subtle beauty and interesting social behavior in the community aquarium.
care_tips: Keep black phantom tetras in groups of at least six, with a balanced mix of males and females to observe their fascinating display behaviors. Males will frequently spar with each other in harmless fin-spreading contests. They prefer soft, slightly acidic water at 72-82°F with some tannins from driftwood or dried leaves. A dark substrate and background make their subtle coloring and dramatic fin displays stand out. They are peaceful with other species and make excellent companions for other tetras, rasboras, and corydoras. Feed a varied diet of quality flakes and frozen foods.

name: Lemon Tetra
description: The lemon tetra is an understated yet charming fish native to the Tapajos River basin in Brazil. Its body is a translucent lemony-yellow that becomes more vibrant with age and good care, complemented by a brilliantly colored eye featuring a striking red upper half. The front edges of its dorsal and anal fins display a bold black and yellow contrast. Lemon tetras are often overlooked in stores where young specimens appear washed out, but well-conditioned adults in a mature tank develop surprisingly rich coloring. They are peaceful, active schooling fish that occupy the mid-water column and mix well with virtually any gentle community species.
care_tips: Lemon tetras are hardy and adaptable, doing well in a range of conditions from slightly acidic to neutral water at 72-82°F. Keep them in schools of at least six, as their coloring improves significantly when they feel secure in a group. A mature, well-planted tank with a dark substrate brings out the best yellow tones. Young specimens in stores often look pale, but their color develops over time with proper nutrition. Feed quality flakes supplemented with frozen foods, and include some vegetable-based foods in their diet. They are excellent beginner tetras that reward patient keepers with increasingly beautiful coloring.

name: Bleeding Heart Tetra
description: The bleeding heart tetra is a large, elegant tetra from the upper Amazon basin in Colombia and Peru. It gets its evocative name from a vivid red spot on its flanks that resembles a bleeding heart, set against a pinkish-silver body. Males develop dramatically extended dorsal and anal fins that they use in impressive display rituals. These are robust tetras that reach about 3 inches, making them one of the larger commonly kept tetra species. Bleeding heart tetras are moderately active schoolers that prefer the mid to lower water levels, and their combination of size, color, and interesting behavior makes them a compelling choice for larger community setups.
care_tips: Bleeding heart tetras need a spacious tank of at least 30 gallons for a proper school, as they are larger and more active than many tetras. Keep them in groups of at least six in soft, acidic water at 73-82°F. They are somewhat sensitive to water quality and do best in mature, well-maintained tanks with consistent parameters. Males may display aggressively toward each other with extended fins but rarely cause injury. Provide a mix of open water and planted retreats. Feed high-quality flakes, pellets, and frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. They can be sensitive to stress during acclimation.

name: Buenos Aires Tetra
description: The Buenos Aires tetra is a robust, active fish from the rivers of Argentina, Brazil, and Paraguay in the Rio de la Plata basin. It has a silvery body with a distinctive blue-black horizontal stripe and red-orange fins that become more vivid in well-conditioned specimens. Buenos Aires tetras are among the largest and hardiest commonly kept tetras, reaching about 3 inches. They are energetic, fast-swimming fish with a reputation for being somewhat boisterous and for enthusiastically eating live plants. While this makes them unsuitable for delicate planted aquascapes, they excel in tanks with artificial plants or hardy species like Java fern and Anubias.
care_tips: Buenos Aires tetras are exceptionally hardy and tolerate a wide temperature range of 64-82°F, making them suitable for unheated tanks in moderate climates. Keep them in groups of at least six, as smaller groups tend to nip tankmates. Be aware that they will devour most live plants, so use hardy species like Java fern, Anubias, or artificial decorations. Pair them with robust, similarly sized fish, as they can be too boisterous for small or delicate species. They are enthusiastic eaters that accept virtually any food. Their hardiness and active nature make them excellent fish for beginners who do not plan on keeping a planted tank.

name: Silvertip Tetra
description: The silvertip tetra is a lively, warmly colored fish from the São Francisco River basin in eastern Brazil. Its body is a rich golden-copper tone, and the tips of each fin are highlighted with bright white or silver, giving the species its name. Males are more intensely colored than females and develop a deeper copper hue. Silvertip tetras are active, fast-swimming schoolers that occupy the upper and middle water levels, creating a flash of golden movement across the aquarium. They are slightly more assertive than many small tetras, which makes them effective dither fish for cichlids while still being suitable for peaceful community setups.
care_tips: Keep silvertip tetras in groups of at least six, as smaller groups may become nippy toward other species. They prefer slightly acidic to neutral water at 72-82°F and are quite adaptable to different conditions. Provide plenty of open swimming space alongside planted areas for retreating. Their golden-copper coloring looks best against a dark substrate and under warm-toned lighting. Feed a varied diet of quality flakes, micro-pellets, and frozen foods. They are active and sometimes boisterous, so avoid housing them with very timid or long-finned species. A planted tank with moderate current suits them well.

name: Red Eye Tetra
description: The red eye tetra is a sturdy, moderately sized fish from the rivers of South America, found across a wide range from Paraguay and eastern Bolivia to Brazil and Argentina. Its most distinctive feature is its brilliant red upper eye, which contrasts sharply with its silvery body and black tail base marking. Red eye tetras are active, confident schoolers that bring reliable movement and a flash of color to mid and upper water levels. They are among the hardiest tetra species, tolerating a wide range of temperatures and water conditions. Their moderate size and robust constitution make them suitable companions for a variety of community fish, including some of the more assertive species.
care_tips: Red eye tetras are one of the easiest tetras to keep, adapting to temperatures from 73-82°F and a range of water chemistries. Keep them in schools of at least six in a tank with ample swimming room. They can be mildly nippy in small groups, so larger schools are recommended. Provide a mix of open areas and planted sections. They are not fussy eaters and readily accept flakes, pellets, and frozen foods. Their hardiness makes them a good choice for beginners, and their confident nature makes them effective dither fish for shy cichlids. Maintain regular water changes for optimal health and color.

name: X-Ray Tetra
description: The X-ray tetra, also called the pristella tetra, is a small, translucent fish from the coastal rivers of South America, primarily Venezuela, Guyana, and Brazil. Its nearly transparent body reveals its internal skeleton and swim bladder, giving it the X-ray common name. The dorsal and anal fins feature bold yellow, black, and white banding that provides a surprising splash of color on an otherwise subtle fish. X-ray tetras are found in both freshwater and slightly brackish habitats in the wild, making them unusually adaptable. They are peaceful, unassuming schoolers that add a unique, almost ethereal quality to community aquariums.
care_tips: X-ray tetras are extremely hardy and can tolerate a wide range of conditions, including slightly brackish water. Keep them in schools of at least six at 75-82°F in neutral to slightly alkaline water. They are one of the most peaceful tetra species and mix well with virtually any small, non-aggressive community fish. Their translucent bodies look most striking against a dark background with moderate lighting. Feed standard flake food supplemented with small frozen or live foods. X-ray tetras are excellent fish for beginners and make reliable, long-lived community residents with a lifespan of 4-5 years.

name: Penguin Tetra
description: The penguin tetra is a distinctive schooling fish from the Amazon and Orinoco river basins in South America. It gets its name from the bold black stripe that runs diagonally from its midsection down through the lower tail lobe, combined with its characteristic head-up swimming posture that vaguely resembles a penguin's waddle. The body is silvery with a subtle golden sheen. Penguin tetras are active, peaceful fish that swim with a unique oblique posture, tilted slightly head-upward, which sets them apart from other tetra species. Their interesting swimming behavior and moderate size make them an appealing choice for community tanks looking for something a little different from the usual tetra options.
care_tips: Keep penguin tetras in schools of at least six in a tank of 20 gallons or more. They prefer slightly soft, acidic to neutral water at 72-82°F. Their unique angled swimming posture is normal and not a sign of illness. Provide both open swimming areas and planted retreats. They are peaceful and mix well with other community fish of similar size. Feed quality flakes and pellets supplemented with frozen daphnia and brine shrimp. Penguin tetras are generally hardy and low-maintenance once established. A longer tank with moderate current suits their active swimming style.

name: Swordtail
description: The swordtail is a popular livebearer native to the rivers and streams of Central America, from Mexico to Honduras. Males are instantly recognizable by the elongated lower tail fin ray that forms the characteristic sword extension, which can grow to match the body length. Swordtails come in a wide variety of colors and patterns through selective breeding, including red, orange, pineapple, tuxedo, and neon varieties. They are active, assertive swimmers that occupy all levels of the aquarium. An interesting biological quirk is that older females can sometimes develop male characteristics including the sword and gonopodium, though this sex reversal does not usually result in functional fertility.
care_tips: Keep swordtails in a tank of at least 20 gallons, as they are active swimmers that need space. Maintain a ratio of one male to two or three females to prevent male harassment and aggression between rival males. They prefer moderately hard, alkaline water at 72-79°F. Swordtails are excellent jumpers, so a tight-fitting lid is essential. Feed a varied diet of quality flakes, small pellets, and occasional vegetable matter like blanched spinach or spirulina. They breed readily, with females producing 20-80 fry every 4-6 weeks. If you do not want fry, keep single-sex groups. They mix well with other livebearers and peaceful community fish.

name: Endler's Livebearer
description: Endler's livebearer is a tiny, brilliantly colored fish originally discovered in a single lagoon near Cumana, Venezuela. Males are among the most vividly colored freshwater fish relative to their size, displaying electric combinations of neon green, orange, black, and metallic blue in intricate patterns that vary between individual fish. Pure Endler's strains are considered endangered in the wild, though they are widely bred in the hobby. They are closely related to guppies and will readily hybridize with them, which is why purists keep them in species-only tanks. Endler's are energetic, constantly active fish that dart around the tank displaying to females with rapid bursts of color.
care_tips: Endler's livebearers are hardy and prolific, suitable for tanks as small as 10 gallons for a small colony. Keep them in groups with more females than males to reduce constant male attention. If you want to maintain pure Endler's genetics, do not house them with guppies, as they hybridize freely. They thrive in slightly hard, alkaline water at 72-82°F and appreciate some plant cover. Dense floating plants like Java moss provide essential cover for newborn fry. Feed quality micro-pellets and crushed flakes supplemented with frozen baby brine shrimp. They breed rapidly, so be prepared to manage population growth or find homes for surplus fish.

name: Sailfin Molly
description: The sailfin molly is the largest and most impressive of the commonly kept molly species, native to the coastal brackish and freshwater habitats of the southeastern United States and Mexico. Males develop a spectacular oversized dorsal fin that can be nearly as tall as the body is deep, which they erect in impressive fan-like displays to attract females and intimidate rivals. Wild sailfin mollies are olive to gray with rows of spots, while captive varieties include silver, gold, black, and dalmatian patterns. These are robust, active fish that can grow to 5-6 inches, significantly larger than standard mollies. They are natural algae grazers and spend much of their time browsing surfaces.
care_tips: Sailfin mollies need a spacious tank of at least 30 gallons due to their larger size and active swimming habits. They do best in hard, alkaline water and many keepers maintain them in brackish conditions with a specific gravity of 1.005-1.010, though they adapt to freshwater. Males need space to display their impressive dorsal fins, and multiple males may compete vigorously. Keep at least two females per male to distribute attention. Feed a diet heavy in vegetable matter including spirulina flakes, blanched vegetables, and algae wafers, supplemented with protein foods. They are prone to fungal infections and shimmies in soft, acidic water.

name: Balloon Molly
description: The balloon molly is a selectively bred variety of the common molly with a dramatically rounded, compressed body shape caused by a shortened spine. This unusual body form divides opinion in the hobby, with some keepers finding them charming and others expressing welfare concerns about the deformity. Balloon mollies come in all the color varieties of standard mollies, including black, gold, dalmatian, and white. Their rounded shape gives them a wobbling, somewhat labored swimming style that is distinctly different from normal mollies. Despite their altered body shape, balloon mollies are active and social fish that interact normally with other tankmates and breed readily.
care_tips: Balloon mollies require the same care as standard mollies but are somewhat more susceptible to swim bladder issues due to their compressed body shape. Keep them in hard, alkaline water at 75-82°F with a touch of aquarium salt if other tankmates tolerate it. Avoid strong currents that may challenge their altered swimming ability. Feed small, frequent meals rather than large ones to reduce swim bladder strain, using quality flakes, micro-pellets, and plenty of vegetable matter. Monitor closely for signs of swim bladder disorder and constipation. Provide gentle filtration and plenty of resting spots near plants and decorations.

name: Otocinclus
description: The otocinclus, affectionately called the oto, is a tiny catfish from the rivers and streams of South America, primarily found in southeastern Brazil, Argentina, and Venezuela. At just 1-2 inches, otos are among the smallest catfish species and are cherished for their tireless algae-eating habits. Their streamlined, sucker-mouthed bodies are perfectly adapted for clinging to smooth surfaces while rasping off thin films of algae. Otocinclus are social, gentle fish that pose no threat to even the smallest shrimp or fry. They are widely regarded as the best algae-eating fish for planted tanks, as they consume diatoms and soft green algae without damaging delicate plant leaves.
care_tips: Otocinclus have a notoriously high mortality rate shortly after purchase due to starvation and stress during shipping. Buy only active, well-fed specimens with rounded bellies. Keep them in groups of at least six in a mature tank with established algae growth. A newly set up tank without biofilm will not sustain them. Supplement their diet with blanched zucchini, cucumber, and sinking algae wafers, especially if the tank's algae supply runs low. They need clean, well-oxygenated water at 72-79°F with zero ammonia and nitrite. Never add them to an uncycled or immature tank. Otos are sensitive to medications, so research treatments carefully.

name: Pictus Catfish
description: The pictus catfish is a sleek, silver-bodied catfish covered in striking black spots, native to the warm, flowing rivers of the Amazon and Orinoco basins in South America. Its long, sweeping barbels can extend past the tail fin, giving it an elegant, whisker-like appearance. Pictus catfish are active, primarily nocturnal hunters that use their sensitive barbels to navigate and locate food in dark conditions. Unlike many catfish species, pictus cats are impressive swimmers that patrol the mid and lower water levels with considerable speed. Their sharp pectoral fin spines can become tangled in fine-mesh nets, so always use a solid container when moving them.
care_tips: Pictus catfish need a tank of at least 40 gallons with moderate to strong flow and plenty of swimming room. They are social and should be kept in groups of at least three, though they may eat very small fish and shrimp. Provide caves and driftwood for daytime hiding, and expect increased activity after the lights go out. Their long barbels are sensitive and can be damaged by sharp substrate, so use sand or smooth gravel. Feed sinking pellets, frozen bloodworms, and occasional live foods in the evening. Pictus catfish have sharp pectoral spines, so use a container rather than a net to avoid entanglement and injury.

name: Glass Catfish
description: The glass catfish, also known as the phantom catfish, is a mesmerizing transparent fish from the rivers of Thailand and Southeast Asia. Its body is almost completely see-through, revealing its skeleton, organs, and swim bladder in stunning detail. Glass catfish are unusual among catfish in that they are active mid-water schoolers rather than bottom-dwellers, hovering in place against a gentle current with subtle body undulations. They are entirely peaceful and somewhat delicate, preferring the company of their own kind in quiet, well-planted aquariums. When stressed or ill, their transparent bodies become cloudy or milky, providing an immediate visual indicator of their condition.
care_tips: Keep glass catfish in groups of at least five, as solitary specimens become extremely stressed and often refuse to eat. They need a calm tank with gentle flow, plenty of plants, and no aggressive tankmates. Position them away from boisterous species like barbs and large tetras. They prefer soft, slightly acidic water at 75-80°F and are sensitive to water quality fluctuations. Feed small frozen foods like bloodworms, daphnia, and brine shrimp, as they may initially refuse dry foods. Glass catfish need time to acclimate and may hide for several days after being introduced to a new tank. Their transparency should be clear, not cloudy.

name: Upside-Down Catfish
description: The upside-down catfish is a fascinating fish from the Congo River basin in central Africa, famous for its habit of swimming and feeding belly-up. This inverted swimming behavior is an adaptation for feeding on insect larvae and algae on the undersides of broad leaves and submerged logs. Their coloring is reversed compared to most fish: the belly is darker than the back, providing camouflage when viewed from below against the dark bottom. Upside-down catfish belong to the family Mochokidae and are one of several species that exhibit this remarkable behavior, though Synodontis nigriventris is the most commonly kept. They are peaceful, social fish with engaging personality.
care_tips: Keep upside-down catfish in groups of at least three, as they are social and more active in company. Provide plenty of caves, driftwood, and broad-leaved plants for them to rest under in their inverted position. They are primarily nocturnal and will be most active after the lights go out, though they gradually become bolder and more visible during daylight in a well-established tank. Feed sinking pellets and frozen foods in the evening. They prefer slightly soft to neutral water at 75-82°F. Their upside-down swimming is completely normal and not a sign of illness. They are hardy and long-lived, often surviving 15 years or more in captivity.

name: Panda Corydoras
description: The panda corydoras is an endearing small catfish from the clear, cool mountain streams of Peru's Ucayali River system. Its creamy-white body is adorned with three distinctive black patches: one over each eye and one at the base of the tail, creating a pattern reminiscent of a giant panda, which gives it its beloved common name. Panda corys are active, social bottom-dwellers that spend their time bustling about the substrate in search of food particles. They are one of the most popular corydoras species in the hobby, combining charming looks with a gentle, community-friendly temperament. Like all corydoras, they occasionally dash to the surface to gulp air, which is perfectly normal.
care_tips: Panda corydoras prefer cooler water than many tropical fish, thriving at 68-77°F, which makes them excellent companions for species that prefer similar temperatures. Keep them in groups of at least six on a smooth sand substrate that protects their delicate barbels. They are somewhat more sensitive than other cory species and do best in mature, well-cycled tanks with stable parameters. Feed sinking pellets, wafers, and frozen foods, ensuring food reaches the bottom. Avoid medications containing copper, as corydoras are highly sensitive to it. Regular water changes and clean substrate are essential, as they spend all their time on the bottom where waste accumulates.

name: Bronze Corydoras
description: The bronze corydoras is one of the original and most widely kept corydoras species, native to the rivers and streams of South America from Trinidad to the Rio de la Plata basin. Its armored body displays a warm bronze-green metallic sheen that catches the light beautifully, and an albino variant with white bodies and red eyes is equally popular. Bronze corys are the classic beginner corydoras, combining exceptional hardiness with engaging social behavior. They are active bottom-dwellers that move in coordinated groups, constantly sifting through the substrate with their sensitive barbels. Bronze corydoras have been bred in captivity for over a century, resulting in one of the most domesticated freshwater fish species available.
care_tips: Bronze corydoras are among the hardiest catfish available, tolerating temperatures from 68-82°F and a range of water conditions. Keep them in groups of at least six on a sand or smooth fine-gravel substrate. They are energetic foragers that help keep the tank bottom clean but should not be expected to survive on scraps alone. Provide sinking pellets, algae wafers, and frozen bloodworms as a regular diet. They prefer moderate flow and well-oxygenated water. Bronze corys are easy to breed in home aquariums when given cooler water changes that simulate the rainy season. Their hardiness and peaceful nature make them ideal for beginners.

name: Peppered Corydoras
description: The peppered corydoras is a beautifully patterned catfish from the rivers of southern Brazil, Uruguay, and Argentina. Its body is covered in an irregular pattern of dark olive-green to black blotches and spots on a lighter base, creating a pepper-like speckled appearance. Peppered corys are one of the original corydoras species introduced to the aquarium hobby and remain enduringly popular. They are cool-water tolerant, naturally inhabiting subtropical streams that can drop to the low 60s Fahrenheit during winter. Like all corydoras, they are social, bottom-dwelling fish that should always be kept in groups, and they communicate with each other through body language and substrate vibrations.
care_tips: Peppered corydoras are one of the most cold-tolerant tropical fish, comfortable at temperatures from 64-78°F, making them ideal for unheated tanks in moderate climates. Keep them in groups of at least six on smooth sand substrate. They are extremely hardy and forgiving of beginner mistakes, which has contributed to their century-long popularity. Feed sinking pellets, wafers, and frozen foods, and ensure food actually makes it to the bottom before faster mid-water fish consume it. They are easy to breed with cooler water changes and are an excellent introduction to fish breeding for beginners. Regular substrate vacuuming helps prevent barbel erosion.

name: Sterbai Corydoras
description: The sterbai corydoras is a striking catfish from the upper Guapore River in Brazil. It features a rich dark brown to black body covered in an intricate pattern of white spots and reticulations, with distinctively bright orange pectoral fin spines that make it instantly identifiable. Sterbai corys are among the most attractive corydoras species and command higher prices than more common varieties. They are notably more heat-tolerant than most corydoras, thriving at temperatures up to 86°F, which makes them one of the few corydoras suitable for keeping with discus. Their active foraging behavior and bold pattern make them a standout addition to any community tank with appropriate water conditions.
care_tips: Sterbai corydoras are uniquely suited among corydoras for warmer tanks at 77-86°F, making them the go-to bottom-dweller for discus setups and other warm-water communities. Keep them in groups of at least six on fine sand substrate. While slightly more expensive than common corys, they are similarly hardy once established. Feed sinking pellets, frozen bloodworms, and wafers, ensuring food reaches them on the bottom. Their orange pectoral spines are mildly venomous, so handle carefully during netting. Provide hiding spots among driftwood and plants, though they tend to be bolder than many cory species. Regular water changes maintain their vivid patterning.

name: Pygmy Corydoras
description: The pygmy corydoras is a diminutive catfish from the Madeira River basin in Brazil, reaching just about one inch at full maturity. Despite their tiny size, pygmy corys are full of personality, often swimming in tight, synchronized schools in the mid-water column rather than strictly hugging the bottom like larger corydoras species. Their silvery bodies feature a thin, dark horizontal stripe from nose to tail. Pygmy corydoras are one of three miniature cory species, alongside the habrosus and hastatus, and are among the smallest catfish in the world. They are ideal for nano tanks and make excellent companions for shrimp colonies, as they are far too small to threaten even the tiniest shrimplets.
care_tips: Keep pygmy corydoras in groups of at least ten due to their small size and strong schooling instinct. They do well in nano tanks of 10 gallons or more with gentle filtration and fine sand substrate. Unlike larger corydoras, pygmy corys frequently swim in the mid-water column and should be provided with resting spots on broad leaves and driftwood throughout the tank. They are sensitive to water quality and need mature, stable tanks with low nitrates. Feed crushed flakes, micro-pellets, and frozen baby brine shrimp. They are excellent companions for cherry shrimp and other dwarf shrimp species. Avoid housing with any fish large enough to eat them.

name: Julii Corydoras
description: The julii corydoras is an elegantly patterned catfish from the coastal rivers of northeastern Brazil. Its body features a beautiful pattern of small, distinct dark spots on a light base, with a bold dark stripe along the lateral line. True julii corydoras are actually quite rare in the aquarium trade; most fish sold as julii are actually the similar-looking Corydoras trilineatus, which has spots that tend to connect into reticulated lines. Regardless of exact identification, these are charming, hardy bottom-dwellers with the same sociable personality as all corydoras. They are popular for their attractive spotted pattern and reliable, peaceful temperament in community settings.
care_tips: Keep julii corydoras in groups of at least six on smooth sand or fine-gravel substrate at 73-79°F. They are hardy, adaptable fish that do well in most community setups. If purchasing, be aware that true Corydoras julii are rare and most specimens sold under this name are C. trilineatus, which is equally attractive and easy to care for. Feed sinking pellets, wafers, and frozen foods, ensuring food reaches them past faster-eating mid-water fish. Provide driftwood and plants for hiding spots. Regular substrate maintenance is important since they spend all their time on the bottom. They are easy to keep and breed, making them great for beginners interested in catfish.

name: Discus
description: The discus is widely regarded as the king of freshwater aquarium fish, native to the calm, warm, blackwater tributaries of the Amazon River basin. Their distinctive round, laterally compressed bodies and extraordinary color patterns have made them objects of fascination for generations of aquarists. Wild discus come in three main species with varied earth tones of brown, green, and blue, while decades of selective breeding have produced dazzling varieties including pigeon blood, turquoise, snakeskin, and solid red. Discus are social, intelligent fish that form complex hierarchies within their groups and can recognize individual humans. Their demanding care requirements and stunning beauty have made them the benchmark against which serious fishkeepers measure their skills.
care_tips: Discus require warm water at 82-88°F, which limits compatible tankmates to heat-tolerant species like cardinal tetras and sterbai corydoras. Keep them in groups of at least five in a tank of 55 gallons or larger with very clean water. Nitrates should stay below 15 ppm, requiring frequent water changes of 25-50% multiple times per week. They are sensitive to stress, so place the tank in a low-traffic area and avoid sudden movements near the aquarium. Feed a high-protein diet of quality pellets, frozen bloodworms, and beef heart mix two to three times daily. Young discus need frequent feeding for proper growth. They are susceptible to internal parasites and bacterial infections, so quarantine all new fish thoroughly.

name: Cockatoo Dwarf Cichlid
description: The cockatoo dwarf cichlid is a colorful, personality-filled fish from the shallow streams and flooded areas of the Amazon basin in Peru and Colombia. Males are dramatically more colorful than females, displaying extended dorsal fin rays reminiscent of a cockatoo's crest, paired with vivid orange, red, and blue coloring. Females are smaller and yellow with dark markings. This species is one of the most popular apistogramma species in the hobby due to its relative hardiness and willingness to breed in aquariums. Males are territorial and maintain small harems of females, each defending her own cave nest. The combination of vivid color, interesting breeding behavior, and moderate care requirements makes this a gateway fish for keepers interested in dwarf cichlids.
care_tips: Provide each female cockatoo dwarf cichlid with her own cave or coconut shell hiding spot, as breeding females become fiercely territorial around their nest. A single male can be kept with two to three females in a 20-gallon tank with broken sight lines using plants and driftwood. They prefer soft, slightly acidic water at 75-82°F with a sandy substrate for their natural sifting behavior. Feed high-quality pellets, frozen bloodworms, and brine shrimp. Females turn bright yellow when ready to spawn and will aggressively defend their eggs and fry from all tankmates including the male. They are more adaptable to different water parameters than many apistogramma species.

name: Borelli's Dwarf Cichlid
description: Borelli's dwarf cichlid is a peaceful, beautifully colored fish from the streams and wetlands of southern Brazil, Paraguay, and northern Argentina. Males display a soft blue body with a golden-yellow face and head, creating a lovely pastel color combination. They are one of the more mild-mannered apistogramma species, making them suitable for community tanks with other small, peaceful fish. Borelli's dwarf cichlids are notably more cold-tolerant than most tropical fish, naturally experiencing temperatures in the low 60s during winter in their subtropical habitat. Their gentle demeanor and attractive coloring have earned them a devoted following among dwarf cichlid enthusiasts.
care_tips: Borelli's dwarf cichlids are hardier and more cold-tolerant than most apistogramma species, doing well at 68-79°F. They prefer soft, slightly acidic water but adapt to moderate hardness. Provide caves and dense planting with a sandy substrate in a tank of at least 15 gallons. Males are less aggressive than many apistogramma species and can sometimes be kept in pairs rather than harems. Feed quality micro-pellets, frozen bloodworms, and brine shrimp. They are generally peaceful enough for community tanks with small tetras and corydoras. Breeding behavior is typical of apistogramma, with females guarding eggs in caves and leading fry around the tank.

name: Kribensis
description: The kribensis is a small, colorful cichlid from the rivers and streams of Nigeria and Cameroon in West Africa. Females are often more colorful than males, developing a vivid cherry-red belly during breeding season, which is unusual in the cichlid world. Males are larger with more elongated fins and pointed dorsal and anal fin tips. Kribensis are cave-spawning cichlids that form devoted breeding pairs, with both parents actively guarding and raising their fry in a fascinating display of parental care. They are one of the easiest cichlids to breed in home aquariums and provide a wonderful introduction to cichlid breeding behavior. Their moderate size and relative peacefulness make them suitable for many community setups.
care_tips: Provide kribensis pairs with caves made from coconut shells, clay pots, or stacked rocks in a tank of at least 20 gallons. They prefer slightly soft, acidic water at 75-82°F, though they adapt to a range of conditions. During breeding, pairs become territorial and will chase other fish away from their nesting area, so provide ample space and hiding spots for other tankmates. They are omnivorous and accept most foods including pellets, flakes, frozen bloodworms, and brine shrimp. The sex ratio of fry is influenced by pH, with lower pH producing more females. Kribensis are hardy and long-lived, often reaching 5 years or more.

name: Oscar
description: The oscar is a large, intelligent cichlid from the Amazon basin in South America, widely regarded as one of the most personable freshwater fish available. Oscars can grow to 14 inches and are known for their dog-like behavior, including recognizing their owners, begging for food, and even allowing themselves to be petted. Wild oscars are olive-green with orange ringed spots, while captive varieties include tiger, red, albino, and lemon patterns. They are powerful, messy predators that rearrange their tanks by moving substrate, uprooting plants, and repositioning decorations to suit their preferences. Oscars are long-lived fish that can survive over 15 years, requiring a significant commitment from their keepers.
care_tips: Oscars need a large tank of at least 75 gallons for a single fish, with 125 gallons or more recommended for pairs. They are extremely messy eaters that produce heavy bioload, requiring powerful filtration rated for double the tank volume and weekly water changes of 30-50%. Feed a varied diet of quality cichlid pellets as a staple supplemented with frozen foods and occasional live treats, but avoid feeding feeder goldfish, which offer poor nutrition and can transmit parasites. Use sand substrate and minimal decorations, as oscars will rearrange everything. They are susceptible to hole-in-the-head disease, which is linked to poor water quality and vitamin deficiency.

name: Convict Cichlid
description: The convict cichlid is a tough, prolific breeder from the lakes and streams of Central America, ranging from Guatemala to Costa Rica. Its common name comes from the bold black vertical bars on a gray body that suggest prison stripes. Convicts are among the easiest cichlids to breed, forming devoted pairs that aggressively defend their territory and offspring against all comers, regardless of size difference. Both parents participate in brood care, and fry can often be seen following their parents around the tank in a tight cloud. Convict cichlids are hardy, adaptable, and full of personality, but their aggressive breeding behavior and territorial nature require careful tankmate selection.
care_tips: Convict cichlids can be kept in a 30-gallon tank for a single pair, but larger is better when they start breeding, as they become extremely aggressive toward all other fish. Provide caves and rocky territories with a sand or fine gravel substrate. They thrive across a wide range of conditions from 72-82°F and pH 6.5-8.0. Convicts are omnivorous and accept virtually any food, including pellets, flakes, frozen foods, and vegetables. Be prepared for them to breed frequently and prolifically. If you do not want constant breeding, keep a single fish or same-sex group. Their aggression during breeding should not be underestimated, even toward much larger tankmates.

name: Jack Dempsey
description: The Jack Dempsey cichlid is a robust, powerful fish named after the famous 1920s heavyweight boxing champion due to its aggressive nature and strong facial features. Native to the slow-moving waters of Mexico, Belize, Guatemala, and Honduras, it is one of the classic large New World cichlids. Wild-type Jack Dempseys are dark olive to gray with iridescent blue and green spangles that intensify with age and mood. The electric blue Jack Dempsey, a naturally occurring color morph selectively bred for enhanced blue coloring, has become extremely popular for its stunning metallic blue appearance. These are intelligent, long-lived fish that can reach 10 inches and develop distinct personalities.
care_tips: Jack Dempseys need a tank of at least 55 gallons for a single fish, with 75 gallons or more for a pair. They are territorial and aggressive, especially during breeding, so provide robust decorations like rocks and driftwood to create territory boundaries. Use sand or fine gravel substrate, as they like to dig. Feed quality cichlid pellets as a staple with frozen foods and occasional earthworms. Water temperature should be 72-86°F with moderate flow. The electric blue variant is generally less aggressive but more delicate than the standard form. Avoid housing with significantly smaller fish that could become prey. Strong filtration and regular water changes are essential due to their heavy bioload.

name: Electric Blue Acara
description: The electric blue acara is a stunningly colored cichlid believed to be a selectively bred variant of the blue acara, originally from the rivers of Central and South America. Its entire body is covered in a brilliant, metallic electric blue that makes it one of the most visually striking freshwater fish available. Unlike many cichlids of similar size, electric blue acaras are remarkably peaceful for their family, earning them the reputation as the ideal cichlid for community tanks. They are intelligent fish that quickly learn to recognize their keepers and will approach the glass at feeding time. Their manageable size, gorgeous coloring, and gentle temperament have made them enormously popular in recent years.
care_tips: Electric blue acaras are one of the most community-friendly cichlids, coexisting peacefully with most fish too large to eat. Keep them in a tank of at least 30 gallons with sand substrate for their natural sifting and digging behavior. They prefer neutral to slightly acidic water at 72-82°F. Provide rocks and driftwood for territory markers and hiding spots. Feed quality cichlid pellets supplemented with frozen bloodworms, brine shrimp, and krill. They may eat very small fish and shrimp, so choose tankmates of appropriate size. Pairs form strong bonds and are relatively easy to breed. Maintain good water quality, as their vivid blue coloring can fade with poor conditions.

name: Firemouth Cichlid
description: The firemouth cichlid is a charismatic fish from the rivers and cenotes of Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula and northern Central America. It gets its common name from the brilliant red-orange coloring on its throat and belly, which it displays by extending its gill covers outward in an impressive threat display that makes it appear much larger than it actually is. This bluffing behavior is largely for show, as firemonths are actually one of the less aggressive Central American cichlids. Their base coloring is a soft gray-blue with darker vertical banding, complementing the fiery red underside. Firemouth cichlids are hardy, moderately sized fish with interesting social behavior that makes them rewarding to observe.
care_tips: Firemouth cichlids need a tank of at least 30 gallons for a single fish or 55 gallons for a pair, with sand substrate that allows them to sift and dig. They prefer slightly alkaline water at 75-86°F. Despite their dramatic threat displays, firemonths are relatively mild-mannered and can coexist with robust community fish like larger tetras, barbs, and other medium cichlids. Provide caves and territories with rocks and driftwood. Feed quality cichlid pellets, frozen bloodworms, and brine shrimp. Pairs become territorial when breeding and may dig large pits in the substrate. Their gill-flaring displays are normal social behavior, not a sign of aggression that should concern keepers.

name: Severum
description: The severum is a large, disc-shaped cichlid from the Amazon basin and rivers of northern South America, sometimes called the poor man's discus for its similar body shape and manageable care requirements. Wild severum are olive-green to gold with subtle dark vertical banding, while captive breeding has produced stunning varieties including gold, red shoulder, and rotkeil (red-headed) forms. Severums are intelligent, personable fish that develop individual personalities and readily interact with their keepers. Despite reaching up to 10 inches, they are among the more peaceful large cichlids, making them suitable for community tanks with appropriately sized tankmates. Their combination of beauty, personality, and relative ease of care makes them a popular choice for keepers seeking a large, engaging centerpiece fish.
care_tips: Severums need a large tank of at least 55 gallons, with 75 gallons or more preferred for adult fish or pairs. They are one of the few large cichlids that can be kept in planted tanks, as they are less destructive than oscars or Jack Dempseys, though they may nibble on soft plants. Provide driftwood and some rocky structures for territory. Feed quality cichlid pellets, frozen foods, and supplement with vegetable matter like blanched peas, spinach, and spirulina, as they are more herbivorous than many cichlids. Keep water temperature at 75-84°F. They are generally peaceful but may become territorial during breeding. Pairs can be slow to form but are devoted parents.

name: Yellow Lab Cichlid
description: The yellow lab cichlid, also known as the electric yellow cichlid, is a brightly colored mbuna from Lake Malawi in East Africa. Its vivid lemon-yellow body with contrasting black dorsal fin edging makes it one of the most recognizable and popular African cichlids. Yellow labs are among the least aggressive mbuna species, which is notable in a group of fish known for their combative nature. In the wild, they inhabit rocky shorelines where they pick at algae-covered surfaces. Like all mbuna, yellow labs are maternal mouthbrooders, with females incubating fertilized eggs in their mouths for about three weeks before releasing free-swimming fry. Their bright color, relative peacefulness, and ease of breeding make them an ideal entry point into the world of African cichlids.
care_tips: Keep yellow labs in a species-specific or mbuna community tank of at least 30 gallons with a sandy substrate and plenty of stacked rocks creating caves and territories. They require hard, alkaline water at pH 7.8-8.6 and temperatures of 75-82°F. Maintain a ratio of one male to multiple females to reduce aggression. Feed a primarily herbivorous diet of spirulina flakes, algae wafers, and vegetable-based cichlid pellets, as high-protein diets can cause bloat. Avoid housing with very aggressive mbuna species like kenyi or red zebra that may bully them. Regular water changes are essential, as Lake Malawi cichlids are sensitive to deteriorating water quality.

name: Peacock Cichlid
description: Peacock cichlids are a group of stunningly colored species from Lake Malawi in East Africa, belonging to the genus Aulonocara. Males display some of the most brilliant coloring in the freshwater world, with metallic blues, reds, oranges, and yellows that rival marine fish. Females are typically a more subdued silver-gray. Unlike the rock-dwelling mbuna, peacocks are open-water hunters that hover above the sandy substrate, using their specialized lateral line system to detect tiny invertebrates buried in the sand. They are generally less aggressive than mbuna, making them more suitable for mixed African cichlid communities. Numerous species and regional variants exist, with popular varieties including the OB peacock, strawberry, and sunshine.
care_tips: Peacock cichlids need a tank of at least 55 gallons with a sandy substrate that allows their natural sand-sifting hunting behavior. Provide some rocks for territory but leave open sandy areas for foraging. They require hard, alkaline water at pH 7.8-8.6 and temperatures of 76-82°F. Keep one male per species or color variant to prevent hybridization, with multiple females per male. Feed quality cichlid pellets, frozen brine shrimp, and mysis shrimp. Unlike mbuna, peacocks benefit from a more protein-rich diet. Avoid mixing with highly aggressive mbuna that may bully the more mellow peacocks. Males develop their full coloring over 12-18 months, so be patient with young fish.

name: Jewel Cichlid
description: The jewel cichlid is a fiery and territorial fish from the rivers and lakes of West and Central Africa. During breeding, both males and females develop an intense, brilliant red coloration covered in iridescent blue-green spots that sparkle like jewels, giving the species its common name. Outside of breeding, they are still attractive fish with olive to reddish-brown bodies and scattered iridescent spots. Jewel cichlids are notorious for their extreme aggression, particularly when breeding, and will fearlessly attack fish many times their size to defend their territory and offspring. Despite their challenging temperament, dedicated keepers find their vivid breeding colors and devoted parental behavior deeply rewarding.
care_tips: Jewel cichlids need a tank of at least 40 gallons with robust decorations that create visual barriers and territories.
