They are highly aggressive, especially during breeding, and should only be kept with other robust, assertive fish that can hold their own. Avoid housing with small or peaceful species. Provide sand or fine gravel substrate with rocks, driftwood, and hardy plants like Java fern that can withstand their digging. They accept a wide range of conditions from 72-82°F. Feed quality cichlid pellets, frozen foods, and occasional live foods. If a pair forms, be prepared for extreme territorial behavior. Consider keeping them in a species-only setup if aggression becomes unmanageable.

name: Tiger Barb
description: The tiger barb is an energetic, boldly patterned fish from the rivers of Borneo and Sumatra in Southeast Asia. Its golden-orange body is crossed by four distinctive black vertical bars, creating the tiger-like pattern that gives it its name. Popular color variants include green tiger barbs with a dark, iridescent body and albino tiger barbs with creamy bodies and faint bars. Tiger barbs are notorious fin nippers, but this behavior is almost entirely a result of being kept in too-small groups. In a proper school of eight or more, they direct their boisterous energy into fascinating intra-school hierarchy displays rather than harassing other species. A large school of tiger barbs in constant, active motion is one of the most dynamic displays in freshwater fishkeeping.
care_tips: The single most important rule for tiger barbs is keeping them in large groups of at least eight, ideally twelve or more. In small groups, they become relentless fin nippers that terrorize tankmates. In proper schools, they focus on establishing their own pecking order through harmless chasing and sparring. Even in large groups, avoid housing them with slow-moving, long-finned fish like bettas, angelfish, or fancy guppies. They prefer slightly soft, acidic to neutral water at 74-79°F in a tank of at least 30 gallons with open swimming space. Feed quality flakes and pellets supplemented with frozen foods. Tiger barbs are hardy, active fish that provide endless entertainment when kept correctly.

name: Rosy Barb
description: The rosy barb is a robust, attractively colored fish from the subtropical hill streams of northern India, Bangladesh, and Nepal. Males develop a deep rosy-pink to red body coloring during breeding season, while females remain a more subdued golden-olive. Rosy barbs are among the largest commonly kept barb species, reaching about 4 inches, and are exceptionally hardy, tolerating temperatures as low as 64°F. They are active, peaceful schoolers that bring color and movement to mid-water levels. Their subtropical origin makes them one of the few tropical fish suitable for unheated aquariums in temperate homes, and they are a popular choice for outdoor ponds in warm climates.
care_tips: Rosy barbs thrive in cooler water at 64-77°F, making them ideal for unheated tanks and compatible with other cool-water species like white cloud mountain minnows and peppered corydoras. Keep them in schools of at least six in a tank of 30 gallons or more. They are generally peaceful but may nip at very slow-moving or long-finned fish. Males show their best rosy coloring in the presence of females and when fed a varied diet including quality flakes, pellets, and frozen foods. They are enthusiastic eaters that may consume soft-leaved plants, so use hardy species like Java fern and Anubias. Rosy barbs are extremely hardy and excellent for beginners.

name: Gold Barb
description: The gold barb, also called the Chinese barb, is a peaceful, golden-colored fish originally from the Red River basin in China and Vietnam. Its warm golden-yellow body is accented with small dark spots and patches, and males develop more intense coloring during breeding. Gold barbs are selectively bred from the wild green barb, which has a more olive-toned body. They are among the most peaceful barb species, lacking the nipping tendencies of tiger barbs, making them excellent community fish. Gold barbs are active, mid-water schoolers that tolerate a wide range of temperatures and conditions. Their undemanding nature and attractive warm coloring have made them a reliable staple of the community fish hobby.
care_tips: Gold barbs are extremely adaptable, tolerating temperatures from 64-75°F, which makes them suitable for unheated tanks and outdoor ponds in warm climates. Keep them in schools of at least six in a 20-gallon or larger tank. They are peaceful and rarely nip fins, making them one of the safest barb species for community tanks with long-finned fish. Feed quality flakes and pellets supplemented with frozen or live foods. They prefer a planted tank with some open swimming space and moderate current. Gold barbs are hardy, disease-resistant, and tolerant of beginner mistakes. They pair well with other peaceful community fish of similar size.

name: Denison Barb
description: The Denison barb, also known as the roseline shark or red-line torpedo barb, is a strikingly beautiful fish endemic to a few river systems in the Western Ghats mountains of Kerala, India. It features a sleek, torpedo-shaped body with a bold red stripe running from the nose through the eye, a black stripe below it, and a vivid yellow-green flash on the tail. Wild populations are endangered due to overcollection and habitat loss, though captive breeding programs have eased pressure on wild stocks. Denison barbs are fast, active swimmers that need ample space and create a stunning display when kept in a proper school. Their combination of elegant appearance and dynamic swimming behavior has made them one of the most sought-after barb species.
care_tips: Denison barbs are active swimmers that need a tank of at least 55 gallons, preferably longer rather than taller, with strong filtration and moderate to high flow. Keep them in groups of at least six, as they are schooling fish that become stressed when kept alone. They prefer clean, well-oxygenated water at 65-77°F with a slightly acidic to neutral pH. Provide a mix of open swimming areas and planted sections with smooth rocks and driftwood. They are generally peaceful but their fast, boisterous swimming can intimidate very timid species. Feed quality flakes, pellets, and frozen foods. Due to their endangered status, purchase only captive-bred specimens from reputable sources.

name: Odessa Barb
description: The Odessa barb is a vibrant fish originally described from specimens found in a market in Odessa, Ukraine, though it is actually native to central Myanmar. Males are among the most colorful barb species, displaying an intense crimson-red band along their flanks contrasted with iridescent greenish-black scales and a pattern of dark spotting. Females are less colorful with olive tones. For many years, the Odessa barb's exact wild origin was a mystery, but it was eventually traced to streams and rivers in Myanmar's central plateau. They are active, peaceful schooling fish that bring vivid color to the mid-water column without the nipping problems associated with tiger barbs.
care_tips: Keep Odessa barbs in groups of at least six in a tank of 20 gallons or more. Males develop their best red coloring in the presence of females and when fed a varied diet rich in carotenoids. They prefer slightly cool to moderate temperatures at 70-79°F and adapt to a range of water chemistries. Provide open swimming space with some planted areas and moderate current. They are peaceful and make excellent community fish alongside tetras, rasboras, and corydoras. Feed quality flakes, pellets, and frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp to enhance their coloring. Odessa barbs are hardy and relatively undemanding once established.

name: Checker Barb
description: The checker barb is a small, elegantly patterned fish from the rivers of Sumatra and Borneo in Indonesia. Its body displays a checkerboard pattern of dark-edged scales on a warm silvery-pink background, with males developing reddish fins and darker coloring during breeding. Checker barbs are one of the most peaceful barb species, completely lacking the fin-nipping tendencies that give some barbs a bad reputation. They are active mid-water schoolers that add subtle beauty and constant movement to community aquariums. Their gentle nature makes them safe companions for shrimp, small tetras, and even long-finned species, which is unusual among barbs.
care_tips: Keep checker barbs in schools of at least six in a tank of 15 gallons or more. They prefer slightly soft, acidic water at 73-79°F but adapt to moderate conditions. Their peaceful nature makes them one of the safest barb choices for community tanks with delicate or slow-moving tankmates. Provide a planted tank with some floating cover and moderate current. Males display their best coloring when competing for female attention, so include both sexes. Feed quality flakes and micro-pellets supplemented with frozen daphnia and brine shrimp. Checker barbs are hardy and undemanding, making them an excellent choice for peaceful community setups.

name: Chili Rasbora
description: The chili rasbora is one of the smallest aquarium fish in the hobby, reaching barely three-quarters of an inch at full maturity. Native to the blackwater peat swamps of Borneo, Indonesia, it lives in extremely acidic, tannin-stained waters among submerged roots and leaf litter. Despite its tiny size, the chili rasbora displays a vivid ruby-red body with a dark lateral stripe and bright red highlights on the fins. They are true nano fish that thrive in small, well-maintained tanks and are popular among aquascapers for adding living color to small planted setups. Chili rasboras are peaceful, shy fish that do best in species-only tanks or with other tiny, gentle companions.
care_tips: Chili rasboras do best in a dedicated nano tank of at least 5 gallons with very gentle filtration, plenty of plants, and a dark substrate. They prefer soft, acidic water at 68-82°F with tannins from Indian almond leaves or driftwood. Keep them in groups of at least ten, as they are most confident and colorful in larger schools. Avoid housing with larger or boisterous fish that may intimidate or eat them. Feed micro-foods like crushed flakes, micro-pellets, and live or frozen baby brine shrimp and daphnia. They are sensitive to water quality swings, so maintain stable parameters with regular small water changes. A mature, established tank is essential.

name: Celestial Pearl Danio
description: The celestial pearl danio, also known as the galaxy rasbora, is a breathtakingly beautiful nano fish discovered in 2006 in small, spring-fed pools near Hopong, Myanmar. Its deep blue-black body is scattered with pearl-like golden spots resembling a starry sky, while the fins display bold red and black striping. The species caused a sensation when first introduced to the hobby, with many initially doubting its natural coloring was real. Males are more intensely colored and slimmer than the rounder, paler females. Despite concerns about overcollection after their discovery, captive breeding programs were quickly established. These tiny jewels are now a staple of the nano fish hobby and planted aquarium scene.
care_tips: Keep celestial pearl danios in groups of at least eight in a tank of 10 gallons or more with dense planting and plenty of hiding spots. Males can be territorial and chase each other, so provide visual barriers with plants and hardscape. They prefer cool to moderate temperatures at 68-76°F and slightly hard, neutral to slightly alkaline water. Feed a mix of quality micro-pellets, crushed flakes, and frozen baby brine shrimp and daphnia. They can be shy initially but become more confident in well-planted tanks with gentle tankmates. Breeding is relatively easy, with fish scattering eggs among fine-leaved plants and moss. They are popular companions for shrimp in planted nano setups.

name: Emerald Eye Rasbora
description: The emerald eye rasbora is a lively, attractively marked fish from the rivers and streams of Malaysia and western Indonesia. Its most distinctive feature is its large, emerald-green eye that stands out against a sleek, silvery body marked with a dark lateral stripe and a bright copper-orange patch at the tail base. Emerald eye rasboras are active, mid-water schooling fish that create a flash of silver and green as they swim in tight formations. They are peaceful and hardy, making them an excellent choice for community tanks seeking something slightly different from the more common harlequin rasbora. Their tolerance for a range of conditions adds to their appeal as reliable community residents.
care_tips: Keep emerald eye rasboras in schools of at least six in a tank of 20 gallons or more with open swimming space and some planted areas. They prefer slightly soft to neutral water at 72-79°F with moderate flow. They are hardy and adaptable, tolerating a range of conditions without difficulty. Feed quality flakes and micro-pellets supplemented with frozen daphnia and brine shrimp. They are peaceful and mix well with other small community fish like tetras, other rasboras, and corydoras. Provide a secure lid, as they can be jumpers when startled. Their active swimming pattern and attractive emerald eyes make them a visually engaging addition to any community setup.

name: Scissortail Rasbora
description: The scissortail rasbora is an elegant, moderately sized fish from the rivers and floodplains of Malaysia, Borneo, and Sumatra. It gets its name from the deeply forked tail fin with bold black and white markings that open and close like scissors as the fish swims, creating a distinctive flickering effect. The body is sleek and silvery with a subtle golden lateral line. Scissortail rasboras are active, fast-swimming schoolers that need ample horizontal space and create a beautiful display of coordinated movement. At up to 6 inches, they are among the largest rasbora species and serve as a mid-water centerpiece school for larger community aquariums.
care_tips: Scissortail rasboras need a spacious tank of at least 40 gallons due to their active swimming and larger adult size of up to 6 inches. Keep them in schools of at least six for the best schooling behavior. They prefer slightly soft, acidic to neutral water at 73-77°F with moderate flow. Provide plenty of open swimming space with planted areas along the sides and back. They are peaceful and make excellent companions for other medium-sized community fish. A tight-fitting lid is essential, as they are excellent jumpers. Feed quality flakes and pellets supplemented with frozen foods. They are generally hardy once established but may be sensitive during initial acclimation.

name: Lambchop Rasbora
description: The lambchop rasbora, also known as Espe's rasbora, is a delicate, warmly colored fish from the peat swamps and forest streams of Thailand and Cambodia. It closely resembles the harlequin rasbora but is distinguished by its narrower, more wedge-shaped dark marking that resembles a lamb chop rather than a broad triangle. Its body has a warmer, more copper-orange tone than the harlequin. Lambchop rasboras are gentle, tight-schooling fish that create a lovely warm-toned display in planted aquariums. They are slightly smaller and more delicate than harlequins, making them better suited to smaller tanks and nano setups with other diminutive species.
care_tips: Keep lambchop rasboras in schools of at least eight in a tank of 10 gallons or more. They prefer soft, acidic water at 73-82°F with subdued lighting and plenty of plants. Indian almond leaves and driftwood add beneficial tannins that mimic their natural peat swamp habitat. They are peaceful and make ideal companions for other small, gentle species like chili rasboras, ember tetras, and dwarf shrimp. Feed quality micro-pellets and crushed flakes supplemented with frozen baby brine shrimp and daphnia. They are somewhat more sensitive than harlequin rasboras and do best in mature, stable tanks. A dark substrate brings out their warm copper coloring.

name: Phoenix Rasbora
description: The phoenix rasbora is a tiny, fiery-colored nano fish from the peat swamps of Kalimantan (Indonesian Borneo). Males display vivid orange-red bodies with a dark lateral stripe and black markings, while females are slightly less intensely colored. At just three-quarters of an inch, they are one of the smallest rasbora species and among the tiniest fish available in the aquarium hobby. Phoenix rasboras inhabit extremely acidic, mineral-poor waters stained dark brown by decomposing plant material. They are closely related to the chili rasbora and share similar care requirements. Their striking coloring relative to their miniature size makes them prized additions to carefully curated nano aquariums.
care_tips: Phoenix rasboras require a well-maintained nano tank of at least 5 gallons with very soft, acidic water at 68-79°F. Add Indian almond leaves, alder cones, and driftwood to replicate their blackwater peat swamp habitat. Keep them in groups of at least eight with gentle filtration using a sponge filter. Avoid housing with any fish large enough to eat them. They need micro-foods including crushed flakes, micro-pellets, and live or frozen baby brine shrimp and vinegar eels. Phoenix rasboras are sensitive to water quality and parameter swings, so maintain stable conditions with regular small water changes. A mature, established tank with some biofilm growth provides supplemental grazing.

name: Clown Loach
description: The clown loach is a large, strikingly patterned fish from the rivers of Borneo and Sumatra in Indonesia. Its bright orange body crossed with three bold black wedge-shaped bands makes it one of the most recognizable freshwater fish. Clown loaches are social, playful fish known for their entertaining behaviors, including lying on their sides to rest (which often alarms new keepers who mistake it for illness), clicking sounds during feeding, and playful chasing within their group. They are slow-growing but can eventually reach 12 inches and live for over 25 years, making them a long-term commitment. Clown loaches are one of the most effective snail-eating fish and are often employed to control pest snail populations in aquariums.
care_tips: Clown loaches need a very large tank of at least 125 gallons for a group of adults, as they grow slowly but steadily to 12 inches over many years. Keep them in groups of at least five, as they are highly social and become stressed alone. Young clown loaches can start in smaller tanks but plan ahead for their eventual size. They are prone to ich and are often the first fish in a tank to show symptoms. They are also extremely sensitive to many medications, so use half-doses or heat treatment for ich. Provide sandy substrate, caves, and driftwood for hiding. Feed sinking pellets, wafers, and frozen foods. Water temperature should be 77-86°F.

name: Yoyo Loach
description: The yoyo loach is an active, boldly patterned fish from the clear, flowing streams of Pakistan and northern India. Its common name comes from the Y and O shaped markings on its flanks that spell out YOYO when viewed from the side, though the pattern varies between individuals. Yoyo loaches are energetic, curious fish that spend much of their time foraging along the bottom and investigating every crevice and hiding spot in the tank. They are social fish that establish hierarchies within their groups, sometimes seen stacking on top of each other in favorite hiding spots. Like clown loaches, they are effective snail eaters and are often added to tanks specifically to control pest snail populations.
care_tips: Keep yoyo loaches in groups of at least three, ideally five or more, in a tank of at least 40 gallons. They prefer moderate to strong current, clean water at 75-82°F, and a sandy substrate for their foraging behavior. Provide plenty of caves, driftwood, and plants for hiding, as they can be semi-nocturnal. They are generally peaceful but can be boisterous and may harass very small or timid fish. Feed sinking pellets, wafers, and frozen foods like bloodworms. Yoyo loaches are excellent snail controllers and will quickly eliminate pest snail populations. Cover filter intakes with sponge, as they can be surprisingly slender and flexible. A tight-fitting lid prevents jumping.

name: Hillstream Loach
description: The hillstream loach is a fascinating, flat-bodied fish adapted to life in fast-flowing, oxygen-rich mountain streams of Southeast Asia. Its body is dorsoventrally flattened with broad, suction-cup-like pelvic and pectoral fins that allow it to cling to smooth rocks in torrential currents. From above, it resembles a tiny stingray or a manta ray. Hillstream loaches are primarily algae and biofilm grazers that methodically work their way across every surface in the tank. They require specialized conditions that replicate their fast-flowing natural habitat, which makes them best suited for experienced keepers who can provide adequate water movement and oxygenation. Their unique appearance and interesting behavior make them a rewarding challenge.
care_tips: Hillstream loaches need cool, fast-flowing, highly oxygenated water at 64-75°F, which sets them apart from most tropical community fish. Provide smooth river rocks, a powerhead or strong filter output for current, and lots of surfaces for biofilm and algae growth. They are best kept in a river-manifold style setup designed specifically for rheophilic species. Feed algae wafers, blanched vegetables, and sinking foods placed in the current. Keep them in groups of at least three and provide ample smooth surfaces for grazing territory. Avoid housing with fish that prefer warm, still water. Regular water changes are essential to maintain the pristine conditions they require.

name: Dojo Loach
description: The dojo loach, also known as the weather loach, is a long, eel-like fish from the cool streams and rice paddies of East Asia, including Japan, China, Korea, and northern Vietnam. It gets the weather loach name from its reputation for becoming restlessly active before storms, supposedly sensing barometric pressure changes through its swim bladder. Dojo loaches can reach 10 inches and have a friendly, docile personality that makes them one of the most personable freshwater fish available. They are often described as the dogs of the aquarium world, happily accepting food from their keeper's fingers and resting in the palm of a hand. Their tolerance for cool water makes them suitable for unheated aquariums and even outdoor ponds in temperate climates.
care_tips: Dojo loaches are cold-water fish that prefer temperatures of 50-72°F, making them unsuitable for heated tropical tanks but perfect for cool-water setups and outdoor ponds. Keep them in a tank of at least 30 gallons with sand substrate, as they love to burrow and will sift sand through their gills. Provide hiding spots with PVC tubes, caves, and plants. A tight-fitting lid is absolutely essential, as they are expert escape artists that can squeeze through surprisingly small gaps. Feed sinking pellets, wafers, frozen bloodworms, and earthworm pieces. They are peaceful and social, best kept in groups. Their personable nature makes them entertaining pets that readily interact with their keepers.

name: Zebra Loach
description: The zebra loach is a small, attractively striped fish from the clear streams and rivers of western India. Its body features numerous narrow, alternating bands of dark brown and cream that wrap around the entire body in a zebra-like pattern. Zebra loaches are active, social bottom-dwellers that spend their time foraging along the substrate and investigating every nook and cranny of the tank. They are one of the smaller botia-type loaches, reaching about 4 inches, which makes them more suitable for moderately sized community tanks than their larger relatives. Their peaceful disposition and manageable size make them an excellent loach for community setups where clown loaches would eventually outgrow the tank.
care_tips: Keep zebra loaches in groups of at least four in a tank of 30 gallons or more with a sandy substrate and moderate current. They prefer clean, well-oxygenated water at 73-79°F. Provide plenty of caves and hiding spots using rocks and driftwood, as they are semi-nocturnal and appreciate daytime retreats. They are effective snail eaters and will control pest snail populations. Feed sinking pellets, wafers, and frozen bloodworms after the lights dim. Zebra loaches are generally peaceful with other species but may chase each other during hierarchy establishment. They are sensitive to poor water quality and need regular water changes. Cover filter intakes to prevent entrapment.

name: Dwarf Chain Loach
description: The dwarf chain loach is a small, beautifully patterned fish from the clear, flowing streams of Thailand. Its body features a distinctive chain-like pattern of dark markings on a golden background, with some individuals showing more interconnected blotches and others displaying separate spots. At just 2 inches, they are one of the smallest botia-type loaches and are perfectly sized for smaller community tanks. Dwarf chain loaches are diurnal and far more active during daylight than most loach species, making them more visible and entertaining to observe. They are social, curious fish that interact frequently with each other and constantly explore their environment.
care_tips: Keep dwarf chain loaches in groups of at least six in a tank of 20 gallons or more. They are one of the most daytime-active loach species, so they provide more visible entertainment than nocturnal species. Provide a sandy substrate with smooth rocks, caves, and driftwood. They prefer moderate current and clean water at 72-82°F. Feed sinking micro-pellets, crushed wafers, and frozen foods like baby brine shrimp and daphnia. They are excellent pest snail controllers even in small tanks. Dwarf chain loaches are generally peaceful but maintain a clear social hierarchy within their group with mild chasing. They are sensitive to water quality and need consistent maintenance.

name: Pearl Gourami
description: The pearl gourami is widely considered one of the most beautiful labyrinth fish, native to the lowland swamps and rivers of Thailand, Malaysia, and Indonesia. Its body is covered in an exquisite pattern of pearlescent white spots on a warm brown-orange background, with a bold dark stripe running from mouth to tail. Males develop a fiery orange-red chest and throat during breeding season. Like all gouramis, pearls possess a labyrinth organ for breathing atmospheric air. They are peaceful, elegant swimmers that move through the aquarium with a calm, flowing grace. Pearl gouramis build bubble nests at the water surface and are among the easier labyrinth fish to breed in captivity.
care_tips: Pearl gouramis do best in a tank of at least 30 gallons with plenty of plants, including floating varieties that provide surface cover and support for bubble nests. Keep the water calm with minimal surface agitation to allow comfortable air breathing. They prefer soft, slightly acidic water at 77-82°F. Males can be kept together in spacious, well-planted tanks with multiple territories, but may become aggressive in cramped quarters. They are peaceful community fish that mix well with other gentle species. Feed quality flakes and pellets supplemented with frozen bloodworms and brine shrimp. Avoid boisterous tankmates that may compete for surface access.

name: Honey Gourami
description: The honey gourami is a gentle, small labyrinth fish from the vegetated ponds, ditches, and slow-moving streams of India and Bangladesh. Wild males display a warm honey-gold body that deepens to a rich amber-orange during breeding, while females are a more subdued tan with a brownish lateral stripe. The commonly sold sunset or red honey gourami is a selectively bred color variant with intensified orange-red coloring. Honey gouramis are among the most peaceful of all gourami species and are far less prone to the aggression and disease issues that plague dwarf gouramis. Their small size, gentle temperament, and beautiful warm coloring make them ideal for small, peaceful community tanks.
care_tips: Honey gouramis are perfect for tanks as small as 10 gallons with gentle filtration and plenty of plants, including floating species. They prefer warm, soft water at 72-82°F with minimal current. Males build bubble nests and are devoted fathers. Unlike dwarf gouramis, honey gouramis are not susceptible to iridovirus, making them a much safer purchase. Keep them with other gentle species like small tetras, rasboras, and corydoras. They can be shy initially but become more confident in well-planted tanks with calm tankmates. Feed small pellets, crushed flakes, and frozen foods like daphnia and baby brine shrimp. Avoid housing with boisterous or aggressive species.

name: Moonlight Gourami
description: The moonlight gourami is a large, ethereally beautiful fish from the lowland rivers, swamps, and rice paddies of Thailand, Cambodia, and Vietnam. Its entire body is covered in a silvery, iridescent sheen that glows with a pale greenish-blue luminescence under aquarium lighting, evoking the soft glow of moonlight on water. Males can be identified by their longer, orange-tinted dorsal fins and orange-red pelvic feelers. Moonlight gouramis are peaceful, somewhat shy giants of the gourami world, reaching up to 6 inches. They are gentle despite their size and prefer calm, densely planted environments where they can retreat among vegetation. Their otherworldly shimmer makes them a stunning centerpiece for large, peaceful community aquariums.
care_tips: Moonlight gouramis need a tank of at least 40 gallons with dense planting, floating plants, and subdued lighting to feel secure and show their best coloring. They prefer warm, soft, acidic water at 79-86°F with minimal current and gentle filtration. Their peaceful nature means they should only be housed with non-aggressive tankmates. They can be shy, especially in brightly lit, sparsely decorated tanks. Feed quality flakes and pellets supplemented with frozen bloodworms and brine shrimp. Males build large bubble nests when in breeding condition. Avoid sudden light changes and provide a gradual photoperiod transition. Moonlight gouramis are generally hardy but appreciate stable, warm conditions.

name: Blue Gourami
description: The blue gourami, also known as the three-spot gourami, is a hardy and adaptable labyrinth fish from Southeast Asia, found in a variety of habitats from swamps and marshes to ditches and rice paddies across Thailand, Malaysia, and Indonesia. The name three-spot refers to two dark spots on each flank plus the eye, which together form three spots. Blue gouramis are actually a color variant of the wild-type spotted gourami, bred for their solid blue-gray coloring. Other color variants include gold, opaline, and cosby. They are robust, medium-sized gouramis that can become somewhat territorial as they mature, particularly males. Despite this, they remain one of the most popular and widely available gourami species.
care_tips: Blue gouramis are hardy fish suitable for tanks of 20 gallons or more. They can become territorial, especially mature males, so keep only one male per tank or provide a large, well-planted setup with broken sight lines. They tolerate a wide range of conditions from 72-82°F and moderate to hard water. Provide floating plants for surface cover and bubble nest building. Feed quality flakes, pellets, and frozen foods. Blue gouramis may chase smaller or more timid species, so pair them with robust community fish that can hold their own. They are generally disease-resistant and long-lived. Avoid keeping multiple males in small tanks, as serious aggression can result.

name: Kissing Gourami
description: The kissing gourami is a large, distinctive fish from the freshwater habitats of Thailand, Malaysia, and Indonesia. It is named for its unique protrusible mouth that it extends in a lip-locking kissing motion, which is actually used for sparring with rivals and rasping algae from surfaces rather than any form of affection. Two color forms exist: the wild green and the more common pink, which is a leucistic variant. Kissing gouramis can grow to 12 inches in large aquariums, making them one of the biggest gourami species commonly available. They are omnivorous and spend much of their time browsing surfaces for algae and biofilm. Their unusual kissing behavior and size make them an intriguing if demanding aquarium resident.
care_tips: Kissing gouramis need a large tank of at least 55 gallons, with 75 gallons or more recommended as they grow. They can be semi-aggressive, using their lips to lock onto and push other fish, so avoid keeping them with very small or delicate species. Provide a spacious tank with plenty of swimming room and robust plants. They are herbivorous grazers that benefit from algae wafers, blanched vegetables, and spirulina-based foods alongside standard pellets and flakes. Water temperature should be 72-82°F. Their kissing behavior between conspecifics is a form of sparring, not affection. Strong filtration is needed for their heavy bioload. They can live 20 years or more with proper care.

name: Sparkling Gourami
description: The sparkling gourami is a tiny, jewel-like labyrinth fish from the shallow, densely vegetated waters of Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Laos. Its body is covered in iridescent blue-green speckles that sparkle brilliantly under light, with red and blue highlights in the fins and a distinctive bright blue eye. Perhaps most remarkable is the sparkling gourami's ability to produce audible croaking sounds using its pectoral fins and a specialized muscle mechanism, earning it the alternate name croaking gourami. These tiny fish can actually be heard from across a room during courtship displays. At just 1.5 inches, they are among the smallest gourami species and are ideal for nano tanks and small planted setups.
care_tips: Sparkling gouramis thrive in nano tanks of 10 gallons or more with dense planting, floating cover, and very gentle filtration. They prefer warm, soft, slightly acidic water at 76-82°F with minimal surface agitation for comfortable air breathing. Males build small bubble nests and croak audibly during courtship, which is a fascinating behavior to observe. Keep them singly, in pairs, or in small groups with adequate space and hiding spots, as males can be territorial in tight quarters. Feed micro-pellets, crushed flakes, and frozen foods like daphnia and baby brine shrimp. They are delicate and should only be housed with other tiny, peaceful species. Listen carefully and you will hear their croaking.

name: Paradise Fish
description: The paradise fish is a brilliantly colored labyrinth fish and one of the earliest tropical fish ever kept in aquariums, first brought to Europe from China in 1869. Males display a stunning pattern of alternating blue and orange-red vertical stripes with flowing, elongated fins in blue and red. They are native to the ditches, rice paddies, and slow-moving waters of East Asia, from China and Korea to Vietnam. Paradise fish are extremely hardy, surviving in temperatures as low as 50°F, which allowed them to survive transport to Europe before the advent of heated shipping containers. Despite their beauty, they are notorious for aggressive, territorial behavior, especially males toward each other and toward other slow-moving or long-finned species.
care_tips: Paradise fish are extremely hardy and can thrive in unheated tanks at 60-80°F, tolerating conditions that would stress most tropical fish. However, males are highly aggressive toward each other and toward long-finned or slow-moving species, so keep only one male per tank and choose robust, fast-moving tankmates. A 20-gallon tank with heavy planting and visual barriers helps manage aggression. They build elaborate bubble nests and are devoted fathers. Feed quality flakes, pellets, and frozen foods. Despite their aggression, their hardiness, stunning appearance, and historical significance make them rewarding fish for keepers who can accommodate their temperament. Avoid housing with bettas, guppies, or other gouramis.

name: Cherry Shrimp
description: The cherry shrimp is a small, vibrantly colored freshwater shrimp selectively bred from the wild Neocaridina davidi of Taiwan. Through selective breeding, color grades range from nearly transparent with red spots (low grade) to deep, opaque cherry-red (Painted Fire Red, the highest grade). Cherry shrimp are the most popular freshwater shrimp in the aquarium hobby, valued for their algae-eating ability, fascinating behavior, and ease of breeding. They spend their time methodically grazing every surface for algae, biofilm, and decaying plant matter. A colony of cherry shrimp in a planted tank creates a living cleanup crew while adding vibrant color. They are excellent indicators of water quality, as they are among the first inhabitants to show stress from deteriorating conditions.
care_tips: Cherry shrimp thrive in a well-cycled, planted tank of at least 5 gallons with stable parameters at 65-80°F and a pH of 6.5-8.0. They are very sensitive to ammonia, nitrite, and copper, so never add them to an uncycled tank or use copper-based medications. Avoid sudden parameter changes by performing small, frequent water changes rather than large ones. Provide hiding spots with moss, plants, and driftwood where molting shrimp can shelter safely. Feed sparingly with shrimp-specific foods, blanched vegetables, and biofilm that grows naturally. Avoid housing with fish large enough to eat them. A healthy colony will breed readily on its own. Use a sponge pre-filter on filter intakes to prevent baby shrimp from being sucked in.

name: Amano Shrimp
description: The Amano shrimp is a medium-sized freshwater shrimp named after the legendary aquascaper Takashi Amano, who popularized its use as an algae-eating cleanup crew in planted aquariums. Native to the streams and rivers of Japan and Taiwan, Amano shrimp are larger and more robust than cherry shrimp, reaching about 2 inches. Their translucent gray-green bodies are marked with rows of dots and dashes along the sides. Amano shrimp are widely considered the most effective algae-eating shrimp available, capable of consuming even tough thread algae that most other shrimp ignore. They cannot breed in freshwater aquariums, as their larvae require brackish water to develop, which means populations must be replenished through purchase.
care_tips: Amano shrimp are hardworking algae eaters best kept in groups of at least five per 20 gallons of planted tank. They are hardy and tolerate a range of conditions at 65-80°F. Like all shrimp, they are sensitive to copper and sudden parameter changes. They are larger and bolder than cherry shrimp, making them less vulnerable to predation from small fish, but still avoid housing with large or aggressive fish. Feed supplementally with algae wafers and blanched vegetables if the tank's algae supply runs low. Amano shrimp cannot breed in freshwater, as larvae need brackish water. They can be escape artists, so maintain a tight-fitting lid. Excellent for controlling algae in planted tanks.

name: Ghost Shrimp
description: Ghost shrimp, also known as glass shrimp, are nearly transparent freshwater shrimp found throughout the waterways of the southeastern United States. Their clear bodies allow observers to watch food moving through their digestive tract and see females carrying developing eggs. Ghost shrimp are commonly sold as feeder shrimp but are fascinating aquarium inhabitants in their own right, displaying active foraging behavior and social interactions. They are among the least expensive and most readily available freshwater shrimp. Multiple species from several genera are sold under the ghost shrimp name, which accounts for some variation in size, behavior, and temperament among individuals from different sources.
care_tips: Ghost shrimp are extremely affordable and hardy, making them ideal for beginners interested in keeping freshwater shrimp. They tolerate a wide range of conditions at 65-82°F. Keep them in groups of at least five in a tank with some plants and hiding spots. They are enthusiastic scavengers that help clean up leftover food and decaying plant matter. While generally peaceful, some individuals can be semi-aggressive toward smaller shrimp species. They breed readily in freshwater, unlike Amano shrimp. Feed a mix of shrimp foods, blanched vegetables, and algae wafers. Ghost shrimp have short lifespans of about one year, so expect regular turnover. They are sensitive to copper and ammonia.

name: Crystal Red Shrimp
description: The crystal red shrimp is a stunning ornamental shrimp bred from the wild bee shrimp of southern China and Hong Kong. Through meticulous selective breeding, this variety displays bold alternating bands of opaque white and deep red on a translucent body. Grading ranges from lower grades with more transparent areas to the prized SSS grade with solid, symmetrical red and white bands. Crystal red shrimp are the pinnacle of freshwater shrimp keeping, commanding high prices for top-grade specimens and requiring more precise water parameters than other common shrimp species. They are the result of a single naturally occurring red mutation discovered by Japanese breeder Hisayasu Suzuki in 1996, from which all crystal red shrimp descend.
care_tips: Crystal red shrimp require very specific water parameters: soft, acidic water with a pH of 5.8-6.8, GH 4-6, KH 0-2, and TDS 100-200. Temperature should be 68-74°F. Use active buffering substrate like ADA Amazonia or similar to maintain acidic conditions. They are extremely sensitive to ammonia, nitrite, copper, and parameter fluctuations. Use remineralized RO water for water changes to ensure consistency. Keep them in a species-only or shrimp-only tank with plenty of moss and biofilm surfaces. Feed sparingly with specialized shrimp foods. Crystal red shrimp are challenging but rewarding for dedicated shrimp keepers. Breeding selectively for higher grades requires patience and culling.

name: Blue Velvet Shrimp
description: The blue velvet shrimp is a striking color variant of the hardy Neocaridina davidi, selectively bred for a rich, velvety blue coloration that ranges from light sky blue to deep cobalt. Like their cherry shrimp cousins, they originate from the wild form found in Taiwan. Blue velvet shrimp are one of the most popular colored Neocaridina varieties, prized for the vivid contrast they create against green plants and natural substrates. They share the same easy-going nature and hardiness as cherry shrimp, making them accessible to beginners while offering a unique color palette. A colony of blue velvet shrimp grazing across a carpet of green moss is one of the most visually appealing displays in nano aquarium keeping.
care_tips: Blue velvet shrimp have the same care requirements as cherry shrimp, thriving in stable, well-cycled tanks at 65-80°F with a pH of 6.5-8.0. They are among the hardiest ornamental shrimp and breed readily in home aquariums. Avoid housing with cherry shrimp or other Neocaridina color variants, as they will interbreed and offspring will revert to dull wild-type coloring over generations. Provide a dark substrate to make their blue coloring stand out. Feed shrimp-specific foods, blanched vegetables, and let natural biofilm grow on surfaces. They are sensitive to copper and sudden parameter changes. Maintain stable water quality with regular small water changes. A sponge filter provides both gentle filtration and a grazing surface.

name: Bamboo Shrimp
description: The bamboo shrimp is a fascinating filter-feeding shrimp from the streams and rivers of Southeast Asia. Unlike most aquarium shrimp that pick at surfaces, bamboo shrimp deploy fan-like appendages from their front legs that they hold open in the current to catch microscopic food particles drifting in the water. They resemble tiny, living satellite dishes when feeding. Bamboo shrimp can reach about 3 inches, making them one of the larger freshwater shrimp available. Their coloring ranges from reddish-brown to tan, and they can change color somewhat depending on their environment and diet. Watching a bamboo shrimp methodically fanning in the current is one of the most unique and calming sights in the freshwater hobby.
care_tips: Bamboo shrimp need moderate to strong current in their tank to carry food particles to their filtering fans. Position them near filter outputs or powerheads where they can establish a feeding station. A tank of at least 20 gallons with good flow at 68-77°F suits them well. If a bamboo shrimp is picking at the substrate instead of fanning, it is not getting enough suspended food and needs supplemental feeding. Add powdered shrimp food, spirulina powder, or crushed flake food upstream of their position. They are peaceful and harmless to all tankmates. Like all shrimp, they are sensitive to copper and sudden parameter changes. Provide hiding spots for molting periods when they are vulnerable.

name: Nerite Snail
description: Nerite snails are small, exceptionally effective algae-eating snails from the brackish and freshwater coastal habitats of tropical regions worldwide. They come in numerous attractive shell patterns including zebra, tiger, olive, horned, and red racer varieties, each with distinctive markings. Nerites are widely regarded as the best algae-eating snails available, methodically grazing every surface in the tank including glass, rocks, plants, and equipment without damaging live plants. A crucial advantage for aquarists is that nerite snails cannot reproduce in freshwater, as their larvae require brackish or saltwater to develop, preventing the population explosions that plague other snail species. Their efficient algae consumption and population control make them the most recommended snail for planted aquariums.
care_tips: Nerite snails are hardy algae eaters that do well in a range of conditions at 72-78°F with moderate to hard water for healthy shell maintenance. They prefer alkaline water with a pH above 7.0 and benefit from calcium supplementation through cuttlebone, mineral blocks, or crushed coral in the filter. While they cannot breed in freshwater, females will still lay small, white, sesame-seed-like eggs on hard surfaces that do not hatch but can be unsightly. These eggs are difficult to remove and are the main complaint about keeping nerites. Ensure adequate algae growth or supplement with algae wafers. Nerites may escape from uncovered tanks, so maintain a tight-fitting lid. Avoid copper-based medications.

name: Mystery Snail
description: The mystery snail is a large, colorful freshwater snail from the rivers and wetlands of South America, popular for its attractive shell colors and entertaining behavior. Varieties include gold, blue, ivory, magenta, and wild-type brown, with shells that can grow to the size of a golf ball. Mystery snails are active, engaging aquarium inhabitants that cruise around the tank using their long siphon tube to breathe at the surface while remaining submerged. They are known for their amusing habit of deliberately dropping from the glass or decorations to float down through the water column. Unlike many snail species, mystery snails reproduce through egg clutches laid above the water line, giving keepers control over population management.
care_tips: Mystery snails need a tank with at least 5 gallons per snail, with hard, alkaline water at 68-82°F and a pH above 7.0 for healthy shell growth. Supplement their diet with calcium through cuttlebone, calcium blocks, or blanched vegetables like kale and spinach. They are omnivorous scavengers that eat algae, leftover food, and decaying plant matter, but should be supplemented with algae wafers and blanched vegetables. Mystery snails lay clutches of pink eggs above the water line, so leave some space between the water surface and the lid. If you do not want baby snails, simply remove egg clutches. They are sensitive to copper and acidic water that erodes their shells.

name: Ramshorn Snail
description: Ramshorn snails are small, flat-coiled freshwater snails found worldwide, named for their distinctive shell shape that resembles a ram's curled horn. They come in a range of colors including red, pink, blue, and brown. Ramshorn snails are simultaneous hermaphrodites, meaning each individual possesses both male and female reproductive organs, and can reproduce rapidly under favorable conditions. They are primarily detritivores, feeding on algae, decaying plant matter, and leftover fish food. While some keepers consider them pests that arrived uninvited on plants, others deliberately cultivate colonies for their cleanup abilities and as supplemental food for pufferfish and assassin snails. Their flat, spiral shells and efficient scavenging behavior make them a useful, if sometimes overabundant, part of the aquarium cleanup crew.
care_tips: Ramshorn snails are extremely hardy and will thrive in almost any aquarium conditions from 65-80°F. They reproduce rapidly when food is abundant, so control populations by reducing feeding and removing excess snails regularly. If overfeeding stops, populations naturally stabilize. They prefer neutral to alkaline water with adequate calcium for shell development. Feed primarily on algae and detritus, supplemented with blanched vegetables and algae wafers if needed. Ramshorn snails are harmless to healthy plants but will consume dying or dead leaves. They are sensitive to copper-based medications. If you want to keep specific color varieties pure, house them separately, as mixed colonies produce random color offspring.

name: Assassin Snail
description: The assassin snail is a small, predatory snail native to the freshwater streams and rivers of Southeast Asia, primarily Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia. Its distinctive cone-shaped shell features alternating bands of chocolate brown and bright yellow, creating a striking appearance. As its name suggests, the assassin snail hunts and eats other snails, making it the most popular biological control method for pest snail infestations in aquariums. Using a tubular proboscis, it bores into the shells of its prey and consumes the contents. Assassin snails reproduce slowly compared to pest snail species, typically laying single eggs in hard-to-reach crevices, which means their populations remain manageable. They are an elegant, effective solution to snail overpopulation that avoids chemical treatments.
care_tips: Assassin snails are the go-to solution for pest snail problems, effectively hunting and eliminating ramshorn, pond, and Malaysian trumpet snail overpopulations. Keep them at 75-80°F in neutral to slightly alkaline water with sand or fine gravel substrate, as they burrow and ambush prey. Once pest snails are eliminated, supplement their diet with frozen bloodworms, meaty sinking pellets, and protein-rich foods. They reproduce slowly, laying single eggs, so population explosions are not a concern. Assassin snails will not harm large snails like mystery snails or nerites. They are peaceful toward fish and shrimp. Avoid copper-based medications. A group of 3-5 assassins can control pest snails in a 20-gallon tank.

name: Malaysian Trumpet Snail
description: The Malaysian trumpet snail is a small, cone-shelled snail native to the freshwater habitats of Southeast Asia but now found worldwide as an introduced species. Its elongated, spiraling shell resembles a tiny trumpet or unicorn horn. Malaysian trumpet snails are unique among common aquarium snails in being livebearers, giving birth to fully formed miniature snails rather than laying eggs. They are burrowing snails that spend much of their time beneath the substrate, emerging primarily at night to forage on the surface. This burrowing behavior provides a valuable service by aerating the substrate and preventing dangerous anaerobic gas pockets from forming. They are both valued helpers and potential pests depending on the keeper's perspective.
care_tips: Malaysian trumpet snails are extremely hardy and reproduce readily, especially in tanks with excess food. They tolerate a wide range of conditions from 65-82°F and adapt to most water chemistries. Their burrowing behavior is beneficial, as it aerates substrate and prevents toxic gas buildup, making them particularly useful in planted tanks with nutrient-rich substrates. Control populations by reducing feeding and manually removing excess snails. They are primarily nocturnal, so a sudden appearance of many snails on the glass at night is normal. They prefer sandy or fine-gravel substrates for burrowing. If populations become excessive, assassin snails are an effective biological control. MTS are sensitive to copper-based medications.

name: Rabbit Snail
description: The rabbit snail is a large, elegant freshwater snail from the ancient lakes of Sulawesi, Indonesia, particularly Lake Poso and the Malili lake system. It gets its common name from its long, drooping face and antenna-like tentacles that vaguely resemble a rabbit's features. Rabbit snails have long, spiral-shaped shells that can reach 4 inches and come in varieties including chocolate, yellow, orange, and gold. They are slow-moving, peaceful snails that graze methodically on algae, biofilm, and decaying plant matter. Unlike many aquarium snails, rabbit snails reproduce slowly, typically giving birth to one or two live baby snails at a time, making population management easy. Their unique appearance and gentle nature have made them increasingly popular in the hobby.
care_tips: Rabbit snails prefer warm, moderately alkaline water at 76-84°F with a pH of 7.5-8.5, reflecting their tropical lake origins in Sulawesi. Provide a sandy substrate for their burrowing and foraging behavior. Supplement their diet with algae wafers, blanched vegetables like zucchini and carrot, and calcium-rich foods for shell health. Add cuttlebone or calcium supplements to maintain strong shells. They reproduce very slowly, giving birth to one or two live babies at a time, so overpopulation is never an issue. Rabbit snails are peaceful and compatible with all community fish and shrimp. Avoid housing with aggressive fish that might harass them. They are long-lived, with lifespans of 3-5 years.

name: Clown Killifish
description: The clown killifish is a tiny, brilliantly colored surface-dwelling fish from the shallow waters of Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone in West Africa. Its body displays bold, alternating bands of cream and dark brown, topped with a spectacular fan-shaped tail fin painted in vivid blue, red, and yellow. Despite being a killifish, clown killis are not annual species and do not require a dry period for their eggs, making them much easier to keep than many killifish. They inhabit the very surface layer of the water, where they hunt tiny insects and surface-dwelling invertebrates. At just 1.5 inches, they are perfect for nano tanks and add stunning color to the often-neglected top water level.
care_tips: Clown killifish are surface dwellers that need floating plants and surface cover to feel secure. Keep them in a nano tank of at least 5 gallons with a tight-fitting lid, as they are skilled jumpers. They prefer warm, soft, slightly acidic water at 73-79°F with very gentle flow. Provide floating plants like water lettuce or salvinia that mimic their natural habitat. Feed small floating foods including micro-pellets, crushed flakes, and live or frozen foods like baby brine shrimp and daphnia. Avoid strong filtration and surface agitation. Males may spar mildly but rarely cause harm. They are peaceful with other tiny species and do well in planted nano community setups.

name: Golden Wonder Killifish
description: The golden wonder killifish is a striking, medium-sized surface predator selectively bred from the striped panchax of India and Sri Lanka. Its body is a vibrant golden-yellow with iridescent scales that shimmer under light, and its large, upturned mouth is perfectly adapted for grabbing prey from the water surface. Golden wonder killifish are active hunters that patrol the top water layer, watching for insects, small invertebrates, and any unfortunate small fish that ventures too close. They are a non-annual killifish species, meaning they live for several years and do not require special drying periods for their eggs. Their bold personality and stunning coloring make them an eye-catching addition to the upper water level.
care_tips: Golden wonder killifish are surface-dwelling predators that will eat any fish or shrimp small enough to fit in their large mouths, so choose tankmates carefully. Keep them with robust, mid-to-bottom-dwelling fish of similar size or larger. They need a tank of at least 20 gallons with a very secure, tight-fitting lid, as they are exceptional jumpers that will leap through surprisingly small gaps. They prefer warm water at 72-77°F with moderate flow. Feed floating pellets, freeze-dried foods, and frozen or live insects like wingless fruit flies and small crickets. Males can be territorial toward each other, so keep one male or provide ample space. They are hardy and adaptable to a range of conditions.

name: Bluefin Notho
description: The bluefin notho is a spectacularly colored annual killifish from the seasonal pools and marshes of Mozambique, Tanzania, and surrounding regions of East Africa. Males display an electric blue body covered in red spots and markings, with brilliantly colored fins in red and blue. As an annual species, bluefin nothos have adapted to a life cycle tied to seasonal rainfall. In the wild, adults live in temporary pools that dry up completely during the dry season, but their eggs survive buried in the mud in a state of suspended development called diapause, hatching when the rains return. This compressed life cycle means they grow rapidly, mature quickly, and live for only about one year, even in captivity.
care_tips: Bluefin nothos have a short lifespan of 12-18 months, so expect a compressed life cycle. Keep them in species-only tanks of at least 10 gallons with a peat or coconut fiber substrate for egg deposition. They prefer warm water at 72-75°F with a slightly acidic to neutral pH. Males are aggressive toward each other, so keep one male with one or more females. Feed high-quality live and frozen foods like brine shrimp, daphnia, and bloodworms to maintain their vivid coloring. Breeding requires collecting eggs from the substrate and incubating them in damp peat moss for 2-6 months to simulate the dry season. They are not suitable for community tanks due to their aggression and short lifespan.

name: Least Killifish
description: The least killifish holds the distinction of being one of the smallest vertebrates in the world, with females reaching about one inch and males barely half an inch. Despite its name, it is not a true killifish but a livebearer belonging to the family Poeciliidae. Native to the southeastern United States, from South Carolina to Louisiana, it inhabits shallow, vegetated margins of ponds, swamps, and slow streams. Least killifish are inconspicuous in appearance, with olive to tan bodies and a subtle dark lateral stripe, but their tiny size and peaceful nature make them fascinating subjects for dedicated nano tank enthusiasts. Females give birth to just 2-5 fully formed fry at a time, one of the smallest broods of any livebearer.
care_tips: Least killifish can thrive in nano tanks as small as 3-5 gallons with gentle filtration and dense planting. They prefer warm water at 68-80°F and adapt to a wide range of water chemistries. Feed micro-foods including crushed flakes, vinegar eels, micro-worms, and live or frozen baby brine shrimp. Their tiny mouths cannot handle standard-sized foods. Keep them in species-only setups or with other truly tiny, peaceful species, as virtually any common aquarium fish is large enough to eat them. They breed slowly compared to guppies, producing very small broods of 2-5 fry every few weeks. Dense vegetation provides essential cover for fry and adults. They are underappreciated gems for dedicated nano fishkeepers.

name: Boesemani Rainbowfish
description: The Boesemani rainbowfish is one of the most strikingly colored freshwater fish, native exclusively to the Ayamaru Lakes region of West Papua, Indonesia. Males display a dramatic two-toned coloring split: the front half of the body is a deep, iridescent blue-gray, while the back half transitions to a vibrant orange-yellow, creating a breathtaking bicolor effect. Females are more subtly colored with olive-silver tones. Boesemani rainbowfish are active, peaceful schooling fish that spend their mornings engaged in spectacular courtship displays, with males flashing their colors and spreading their fins to impress females. Wild populations are endangered due to habitat degradation, making captive-bred specimens an environmentally responsible choice.
care_tips: Boesemani rainbowfish need a spacious tank of at least 40 gallons for a school, with plenty of open swimming space. Keep them in groups of at least six with more females than males for the best displays while reducing male-on-male aggression. They prefer moderately hard, slightly alkaline water at 77-86°F. Males develop their fullest coloring after about 18 months, so be patient with young specimens that may appear drab. Feed quality flakes, pellets, and frozen foods, with color-enhancing foods to bring out their orange tones. Provide strong filtration and good water quality. Morning is the best time to observe their spectacular courtship displays. Purchase only captive-bred fish.

name: Neon Dwarf Rainbowfish
description: The neon dwarf rainbowfish, also known as the praecox rainbowfish, is a small, shimmering schooler from the Mamberamo River system in West Papua, Indonesia. Males display an iridescent neon blue body that flashes brilliantly under aquarium lighting, with vivid red or orange fin edges that intensify during display. Females are less intensely colored but still attractive with a subtle blue sheen. At about 3 inches, they are the perfect size for moderately sized community tanks, offering rainbowfish beauty without the space requirements of larger species. Neon dwarf rainbowfish are active, peaceful fish that engage in morning display rituals, with males swimming rapidly back and forth in front of females with fins fully spread.
care_tips: Keep neon dwarf rainbowfish in groups of at least six, ideally with equal numbers of males and females, in a tank of 20 gallons or more. They prefer slightly alkaline, moderately hard water at 73-82°F with moderate flow and good oxygenation. Their neon blue coloring is most vivid under bright lighting conditions. Feed quality flakes and pellets supplemented with frozen brine shrimp and daphnia for the best fin coloring. They are peaceful and make excellent community fish with other gentle species of similar size. Males display most actively in the morning hours. Provide open swimming areas with planted borders. They are hardy and relatively undemanding for rainbowfish.

name: Turquoise Rainbowfish
description: The turquoise rainbowfish is a vibrantly colored species from the Lake Kutubu region of Papua New Guinea. Males develop a stunning turquoise to blue-green body coloring with contrasting orange or yellow-edged fins and a distinctive bright band running horizontally through the upper body. They are medium-sized rainbowfish that reach about 4 inches and display the active, social behavior characteristic of the group. Turquoise rainbowfish are enthusiastic display fish, with males performing elaborate fin-flashing courtship rituals each morning at dawn. Their vivid coloring and dynamic social behavior make them one of the most desirable rainbowfish species for larger community aquariums.
care_tips: Turquoise rainbowfish need a tank of at least 40 gallons with open swimming space and moderate to strong filtration. Keep them in groups of at least six in slightly alkaline, moderately hard water at 72-77°F. They are active swimmers that appreciate current and well-oxygenated water. Males show their best coloring in the presence of females and rival males. Feed quality flakes, pellets, and frozen foods to maintain their vivid turquoise coloring. They are generally peaceful but males can become boisterous during display. Pair them with similarly sized, active community fish. Morning is the best time to observe their spectacular courtship displays.

name: Madagascar Rainbowfish
description: The Madagascar rainbowfish is one of the most colorful freshwater fish from the island of Madagascar, found in clear, flowing streams and rivers on the eastern side of the island. Males are spectacular, with iridescent silver-blue bodies that flash with green and purple highlights, complemented by vivid red fins. Females are less colorful with olive-silver bodies. Madagascar rainbowfish are active, peaceful schoolers that reach about 6 inches and need spacious tanks to display their full beauty. They are relatively uncommon in the hobby compared to other rainbowfish, partly due to their remote origin and partly because wild populations face significant threats from habitat loss and introduced species on Madagascar.
care_tips: Madagascar rainbowfish need a spacious tank of at least 55 gallons with moderate to strong current and excellent water quality. They prefer slightly alkaline water at 72-77°F with good oxygenation. Keep them in groups of at least six for the best schooling behavior and male displays. Feed quality flakes, pellets, and frozen foods. They are active swimmers that need open space alongside planted areas. Madagascar rainbowfish are generally peaceful but their activity level may stress very timid species. Due to conservation concerns, always choose captive-bred specimens. They are somewhat more demanding than other rainbowfish and best suited for experienced keepers who can provide stable conditions.

name: Red Irian Rainbowfish
description: The red Irian rainbowfish is a large, magnificently colored species from the shallow lakes and streams of Papua, Indonesia. Males develop a deep, warm red coloring over their entire body that intensifies with age and dominance, making mature specimens among the most vividly red freshwater fish available. Females and juveniles are silvery-olive with subtle red hints. At up to 6 inches, they are one of the larger commonly kept rainbowfish species. Red Irian rainbowfish are active, social fish that engage in dramatic morning display rituals, with dominant males showing their most intense red coloring. Their bold color and active nature make them a stunning centerpiece school for large community aquariums.
care_tips: Red Irian rainbowfish need a large tank of at least 55 gallons with ample swimming space. Keep them in groups of at least six with more females than males to reduce competition. They prefer slightly alkaline, moderately hard water at 77-86°F. Males develop their deepest red coloring after about two years, so patience is required with young specimens. Feed color-enhancing foods including spirulina, carotenoid-rich pellets, and frozen brine shrimp to bring out their red tones. Strong filtration and regular water changes maintain the clean conditions they require. They are peaceful community fish that pair well with other large, active species. Provide both open swimming areas and planted sections.

name: Celebes Rainbowfish
description: The Celebes rainbowfish is a delicate, elegant species from the brackish estuaries and freshwater streams of Sulawesi (formerly Celebes), Indonesia. Its translucent, golden-olive body is accented by a prominent iridescent blue-green lateral stripe and distinctive elongated fin rays on the second dorsal and anal fins of males, which create an eye-catching sail-like appearance. Celebes rainbowfish are smaller and more delicate than most other rainbowfish species, reaching about 3 inches. They are peaceful, somewhat timid fish that do best in calm, well-planted tanks with other gentle species. Their subtle, ethereal beauty is best appreciated in a thoughtfully designed aquarium with appropriate lighting.
care_tips: Celebes rainbowfish prefer slightly hard, alkaline water at 72-82°F and historically many keepers added a small amount of salt, though this is not strictly necessary for tank-bred specimens. Keep them in groups of at least six in a tank of 20 gallons or more with moderate flow and plenty of plants. They are timid and should be housed only with other peaceful species. Avoid boisterous tankmates that may outcompete them for food or cause stress. Feed quality micro-pellets, crushed flakes, and frozen foods like daphnia and baby brine shrimp. Males display their elongated fin rays during courtship. They are somewhat delicate compared to other rainbowfish and benefit from stable, consistent conditions.

name: Forktail Blue-Eye Rainbowfish
description: The forktail blue-eye rainbowfish is a tiny, colorful species from the clear, shallow streams and swampy areas of Papua New Guinea. Males display bright yellow bodies with striking blue eyes and a distinctive forked tail fin with elongated upper and lower lobes edged in yellow. At about 2 inches, they are one of the smallest rainbowfish species and are perfectly suited for nano and small community tanks. Forktail blue-eyes are active, personable fish that spend much of their time displaying to each other in the upper water column. Their combination of vivid color, small size, and peaceful nature has made them increasingly popular in the planted nano aquarium community.
care_tips: Keep forktail blue-eye rainbowfish in groups of at least six in a tank of 15 gallons or more with moderate flow and plenty of plants. They prefer slightly alkaline, moderately hard water at 75-79°F. Males display their best coloring and fin extensions in the presence of females and rival males. Feed quality micro-pellets, crushed flakes, and frozen baby brine shrimp and daphnia. They are peaceful and make excellent companions for other small community fish, shrimp, and snails. Provide a mix of open swimming space near the surface and planted areas. Their bright blue eyes are most vivid under good lighting. They are relatively hardy for their small size.

name: Spotted Blue-Eye Rainbowfish
description: The spotted blue-eye rainbowfish, also known as Gertrude's blue-eye, is a tiny, jewel-like fish from the shallow, vegetated waters of Papua New Guinea and northern Australia. Males are adorned with intricate patterns of yellow spots on their bodies and fins, complemented by brilliant blue eyes and dramatically extended fin filaments that they display during courtship. At just 1.5 inches, they are among the smallest rainbowfish and are ideal for nano aquariums. Spotted blue-eyes are delicate, peaceful fish that bring incredible detail and color to small-scale aquatic setups. Males engage in fascinating competitive displays, spreading their ornate fins to their fullest extent while swimming alongside rivals.
care_tips: Spotted blue-eye rainbowfish do best in nano tanks of 10 gallons or more with gentle filtration, dense planting, and moderate lighting to showcase their spotted patterns. Keep them in groups of at least six with more females than males. They prefer slightly alkaline, moderately hard water at 75-82°F. Feed micro-foods including crushed flakes, micro-pellets, and live or frozen baby brine shrimp. They are delicate and should only be housed with other tiny, peaceful species. Males display most actively in the morning. Provide floating plants and surface cover for security. They are more sensitive than hardier nano fish and require stable, mature tanks with consistent parameters.

name: White Cloud Mountain Minnow
description: The white cloud mountain minnow is a small, brightly colored fish originally discovered on White Cloud Mountain near Guangzhou, China, in 1932. Its slender body features an iridescent blue and pink lateral stripe, reddish fins, and a golden-bronze sheen. For decades it was considered extinct in the wild before small populations were rediscovered. White cloud mountain minnows are subtropical fish that prefer cool water, naturally inhabiting clear mountain streams. Popular variants include the golden white cloud and the long-finned form. They are incredibly hardy, peaceful fish that have earned the nickname of the poor man's neon tetra for their similar appearance and schooling behavior at a fraction of the cost and difficulty.
care_tips: White cloud mountain minnows are cool-water fish that thrive at 60-72°F, making them ideal for unheated tanks and outdoor tubs in temperate climates during summer. They actually suffer in typical tropical temperatures above 80°F. Keep them in schools of at least six in a tank of 10 gallons or more. They are peaceful and make excellent companions for other cool-water species like rosy barbs and peppered corydoras. Feed quality flakes and micro-pellets supplemented with frozen daphnia and brine shrimp. White cloud mountain minnows are among the hardiest aquarium fish available and are nearly indestructible for beginners. They breed readily in planted tanks, scattering eggs among fine-leaved vegetation.

name: Leopard Danio
description: The leopard danio is a spotted variety of the zebra danio, native to the same South Asian waters of India, Bangladesh, and Nepal. Instead of the zebra's horizontal stripes, the leopard danio displays a pattern of dark blue-brown spots and speckles scattered across a golden background, creating a leopard-like appearance. It was once classified as a separate species but is now recognized as a color variant of Danio rerio. Leopard danios are just as hardy and active as their striped counterparts, making them excellent beginner fish. A longfin variety with flowing, extended fins adds an elegant twist to this energetic little fish. They share the zebra danio's legendary tolerance for a wide range of aquarium conditions.
care_tips: Leopard danios have identical care requirements to zebra danios. They are extremely hardy and adapt to temperatures from 65-77°F. Keep them in schools of at least six in a tank with plenty of horizontal swimming space. They are very active and benefit from a longer tank rather than a taller one. Provide a tight-fitting lid, as they are accomplished jumpers. Feed quality flakes and micro-pellets with occasional frozen or live foods. They are peaceful schoolers that mix well with most community fish. The longfin variety is slightly slower and more delicate than the standard form. They are among the best fish for beginners and for cycling new tanks using the fishless method.

name: Pearl Danio
description: The pearl danio is an attractive, iridescent fish from the cool mountain streams of Myanmar, Sumatra, and surrounding regions of Southeast Asia. Its body displays a beautiful pearlescent sheen with subtle blue and gold tones, complemented by a vivid orange-red stripe running from the midsection to the tail. Pearl danios are active, graceful swimmers that occupy the upper and mid-water levels with quick, darting movements. They are less commonly kept than zebra danios but offer a more subtle, elegant appearance. Pearl danios naturally inhabit clear, cool, flowing waters and prefer similar conditions in the aquarium. Their iridescent beauty is best appreciated under proper lighting.
care_tips: Pearl danios prefer cool to moderate temperatures at 64-75°F, making them suitable for unheated tanks in most homes. Keep them in schools of at least six in a tank of 20 gallons or more with moderate current and good oxygenation. They are active swimmers that need ample horizontal space. Provide a mix of open swimming areas and planted sections. Feed quality flakes, micro-pellets, and frozen foods. Pearl danios are peaceful and mix well with other cool-water species like white cloud mountain minnows and corydoras. They are hardy and adaptable, though they may struggle in very warm tropical setups above 80°F. A secure lid prevents jumping.

name: Giant Danio
description: The giant danio is the largest commonly kept danio species, reaching about 4 inches, from the clear, fast-flowing hill streams of India, Nepal, and Sri Lanka. Its sleek, torpedo-shaped body is a shimmering blue-green with bright yellow horizontal stripes and iridescent scales. Giant danios are fast, energetic swimmers that create a spectacular display of movement in the upper water levels of the aquarium. They are schooling fish that swim in tight, coordinated groups, darting rapidly back and forth across the tank. Their combination of size, speed, color, and activity level makes them a dynamic centerpiece school for larger community aquariums. They are also commonly used as dither fish for shy cichlid species.
care_tips: Giant danios need a spacious tank of at least 40 gallons, preferably longer than taller, with strong filtration and moderate current to match their active swimming style. Keep them in schools of at least six for natural schooling behavior. They are hardy and adapt to temperatures from 72-81°F. A very secure lid is essential, as they are powerful jumpers. Feed quality flakes, pellets, and frozen foods. Giant danios are peaceful but their fast, boisterous swimming can intimidate very small or timid species. They make excellent dither fish for medium cichlids, encouraging shy species to come out into the open. Their energetic nature makes them one of the most dynamic fish for larger community setups.

name: Longfin Zebra Danio
description: The longfin zebra danio is an elegant variant of the standard zebra danio, featuring dramatically elongated and flowing dorsal, anal, and caudal fins that trail behind it like veils as it swims. It retains the same blue and silver horizontal striping as the standard form, combined with the graceful, flowing fins of the longfin mutation. The extended fins give this normally fast, darting fish a more stately, flowing swimming style while maintaining much of the original's energy and activity. Longfin zebra danios are slightly less robust than the standard form due to their larger fin area, but they retain the species' legendary hardiness and adaptability.
care_tips: Longfin zebra danios share the same basic care requirements as standard zebra danios but benefit from slightly calmer water with less aggressive current, as their extended fins create more drag. Keep them in schools of at least six at 65-77°F. Avoid housing them with known fin nippers like tiger barbs and serpae tetras that may target their flowing fins. They are slightly more susceptible to fin rot than standard zebra danios, so maintain excellent water quality. Feed quality flakes and frozen foods. Provide a secure lid to prevent jumping. They are still very hardy and suitable for beginners who want something slightly more elegant than the standard variety.

name: Gold Ring Danio
description: The gold ring danio is a tiny, warmly colored nano fish from the shallow, slow-moving streams and rice paddies of Myanmar. At just about one inch, it is one of the smallest danio species available. Its body displays a golden-olive tone with a distinctive ring of darker marking around the caudal peduncle, along with subtle iridescent highlights. Gold ring danios are active, schooling fish that occupy the mid-water column with quick, energetic movements despite their diminutive size.
