They are relatively recent additions to the aquarium hobby and are gaining popularity among nano tank enthusiasts who appreciate their active nature and warm, golden coloring.
care_tips: Gold ring danios do well in nano tanks of 10 gallons or more with gentle to moderate filtration. Keep them in groups of at least eight due to their small size and schooling nature. They prefer warm water at 73-79°F with slightly acidic to neutral pH. Provide a planted tank with open swimming areas and some floating cover. Feed micro-pellets, crushed flakes, and frozen baby brine shrimp and daphnia. They are peaceful and make good companions for other tiny species like ember tetras, chili rasboras, and dwarf shrimp. Avoid housing with larger fish that may view them as food. A secure lid prevents their occasional jumping.

name: Siamese Algae Eater
description: The Siamese algae eater is a slender, active fish from the flowing streams and rivers of Thailand and Malaysia. It is widely regarded as the most effective algae-eating fish available to freshwater aquarists, capable of consuming the notorious black beard algae (BBA) that virtually no other fish will touch. Its body is olive-brown with a prominent black stripe running from nose to tail that extends into the tail fin, which distinguishes it from similar-looking imposters like the Chinese algae eater and the flying fox. Siamese algae eaters are peaceful, active swimmers that constantly graze on surfaces throughout the tank. They are a staple recommendation for planted aquarium enthusiasts battling algae problems.
care_tips: Siamese algae eaters are active swimmers that need at least 30 gallons with good flow and open swimming space. They eat black beard algae (BBA), green algae, and other types that most algae eaters ignore, making them invaluable for planted tanks. However, as they grow and age, they may become less interested in algae and prefer commercial foods. Keep them singly or in small groups and avoid housing with similar-looking species that may cause territorial conflicts. Feed algae wafers and blanched vegetables alongside standard foods. They are generally peaceful but can become somewhat territorial as they mature. Temperature should be 75-79°F. Avoid confusing them with Chinese algae eaters, which become aggressive.

name: Flying Fox
description: The flying fox is a sleek, bottom-dwelling fish from the fast-flowing streams of Borneo, Java, Sumatra, and Thailand. It closely resembles the Siamese algae eater but can be distinguished by its more colorful appearance, with a golden-orange stripe above the black lateral line and reddish-tinted fins. Flying foxes are effective algae grazers that spend much of their time rasping biofilm and soft algae from rocks, driftwood, and plant leaves. They are territorial toward their own species and similar-looking fish but generally peaceful with dissimilar tankmates. Flying foxes become more territorial and assertive as they mature, which should be considered when planning long-term community tank compositions.
care_tips: Flying foxes need a tank of at least 30 gallons with moderate current and well-oxygenated water at 73-81°F. Keep only one per tank, as they are territorial toward their own kind and similar-looking species like Siamese algae eaters and rainbow sharks. They are good algae eaters when young but may rely more on commercial foods as they mature. Feed a mix of algae wafers, blanched vegetables, and sinking pellets. Provide plenty of hiding spots with driftwood and rocks. They are generally peaceful toward dissimilar species but may chase fish with similar body shapes. Maintain good water quality with regular changes. They are hardy once established and long-lived.

name: Red Tail Shark
description: The red tail shark, also known as the red-tailed black shark, is a striking fish from the Chao Phraya basin in Thailand, where it is critically endangered in the wild. Its velvety black body provides a dramatic contrast to its vivid red-orange tail fin, making it one of the most visually striking freshwater fish available. Despite the shark common name, it is actually a cyprinid related to barbs and minnows. Red tail sharks are territorial bottom-dwellers that patrol and defend their chosen area aggressively, particularly against similar-looking fish. They are active, engaging fish with bold personalities that can become the dominant character in a community tank.
care_tips: Keep only one red tail shark per tank, as they are highly territorial toward their own species and similar-looking fish like rainbow sharks and flying foxes. A tank of at least 55 gallons with plenty of caves, driftwood, and visual barriers is recommended. They prefer moderate to strong current at 72-79°F. Despite their territorial nature, they generally leave dissimilar species alone, making them suitable for community tanks with robust, non-similar-looking fish. Feed a varied diet of sinking pellets, algae wafers, blanched vegetables, and frozen foods. Red tail sharks are critically endangered in the wild, so all specimens are captive-bred. They can live over 8 years with proper care.

name: Rainbow Shark
description: The rainbow shark is a sleek, dark-bodied fish with vivid red-orange fins native to the rivers of Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, and Vietnam. An albino variant with a white body and red fins is equally popular. Despite the name, rainbow sharks are not true sharks but cyprinids related to barbs. They are semi-aggressive, bottom-dwelling fish that establish and vigorously defend territories against other bottom-dwellers and similar-looking species. Rainbow sharks are active swimmers that patrol the lower levels of the aquarium with purpose and determination. Their combination of striking appearance and bold personality makes them popular centerpiece fish, though their territorial behavior requires thoughtful tankmate planning.
care_tips: Rainbow sharks need a tank of at least 55 gallons with plenty of caves, rocks, and driftwood to establish territories. Keep only one rainbow shark per tank and avoid similar-looking species like red tail sharks and flying foxes. They are most aggressive toward other bottom-dwellers, so stock the lower levels carefully and provide numerous hiding spots. They generally ignore mid-water and surface-dwelling species. Feed sinking pellets, algae wafers, blanched vegetables, and frozen foods at 72-79°F. They are hardy and adaptable to a range of conditions. Rainbow sharks become more territorial as they mature, so plan for their adult behavior rather than their juvenile docility.

name: Common Pleco
description: The common pleco is a large, armored catfish from the rivers of South America, one of the most widely sold but most frequently misunderstood aquarium fish. Sold as small, cute algae eaters in pet stores, common plecos can grow to 18 inches or more and live for over 20 years, quickly outgrowing most home aquariums. Their bodies are covered in bony plates and they sport a broad, flat head with a powerful sucker mouth used to rasp algae from surfaces. Common plecos are primarily nocturnal, hiding during the day and becoming active at night. While they are effective algae eaters when young, larger specimens rely more on supplemental feeding and produce enormous amounts of waste.
care_tips: Common plecos need a very large tank of at least 125 gallons for a fully grown adult. Do not purchase one expecting it to stay small. They produce an enormous amount of waste, requiring heavy filtration and frequent large water changes. Provide large pieces of driftwood, as they rasp on it for dietary fiber and use it as a hiding spot. Feed sinking algae wafers, blanched vegetables like zucchini and sweet potato, and occasional protein foods at night. Temperature should be 72-82°F. If your tank cannot accommodate an 18-inch fish long-term, choose a bristlenose pleco instead, which stays around 5 inches. Never release plecos into the wild, as they are invasive in many regions.

name: Rubber Lip Pleco
description: The rubber lip pleco is a small, practical catfish from the fast-flowing rivers of Venezuela and Colombia. At around 4 inches, it offers all the algae-eating benefits of a pleco without the extreme size of the common pleco. Its body is olive-brown with darker spots and a distinctive rubber-like lip texture used for clinging to rocks and rasping algae in strong currents. Rubber lip plecos are one of the most effective algae eaters relative to their size, methodically cleaning glass, rocks, and decorations without damaging live plants. They are an excellent alternative for aquarists who want pleco-style algae control in moderately sized tanks.
care_tips: Rubber lip plecos are ideal for tanks of 25 gallons or more, staying at a manageable 4 inches. They prefer cooler water at 72-78°F with moderate to strong flow and good oxygenation. Feed algae wafers and blanched vegetables like zucchini and cucumber. Unlike many plecos, they remain enthusiastic algae eaters throughout their lives rather than becoming lazy with age. Provide driftwood for shelter and dietary fiber. They are peaceful and unobtrusive, spending most of their time clinging to surfaces. Maintain clean, well-oxygenated water, as they come from fast-flowing river habitats. They are a much more practical choice than common plecos for most home aquariums.

name: Clown Pleco
description: The clown pleco is a small, attractively patterned catfish from the rivers and tributaries of Venezuela and Colombia. Its dark brown to black body is adorned with distinctive wavy lines and bands of bright orange to cream, creating a clown-like pattern that gives it its common name. At 3-4 inches, the clown pleco is one of the smallest commonly available pleco species, making it suitable for moderately sized aquariums. Clown plecos are wood-eaters that require driftwood as a significant part of their diet, spending much of their time rasping at wood surfaces. They are nocturnal and secretive, typically only emerging from their hiding spots after the lights go out.
care_tips: Clown plecos absolutely require driftwood in their tank, as wood fiber is an essential part of their diet. Without driftwood, they will not thrive. Provide multiple pieces of driftwood along with caves and tight spaces for hiding. They are suitable for tanks of 20 gallons or more at 73-82°F. Unlike bristlenose plecos, clown plecos are not prolific algae eaters, so do not purchase one expecting algae control. Supplement their wood-based diet with algae wafers and blanched vegetables. They are nocturnal and secretive, so do not be alarmed if you rarely see them during the day. Feed at night when they are most active. They are peaceful and harmless to all tankmates.

name: Royal Pleco
description: The royal pleco is a large, impressively marked catfish from the Orinoco and Amazon river basins in Venezuela, Colombia, and Brazil. Its body features bold, wavy dark brown lines on a lighter tan to gray background, with striking red eyes that add to its regal appearance. Royal plecos can reach up to 17 inches, making them among the largest commonly kept pleco species. They are specialized wood-eaters with powerful jaws adapted for rasping and consuming driftwood, processing it with the help of symbiotic gut bacteria. Royal plecos are slow-growing, long-lived fish that can survive for over 25 years. Their impressive size, distinctive pattern, and unusual dietary habits make them fascinating aquarium specimens for dedicated keepers.
care_tips: Royal plecos need a very large tank of at least 125 gallons for adults, with multiple large pieces of driftwood as both shelter and the primary component of their diet. They are obligate wood-eaters and will not thrive without substantial driftwood. Supplement with blanched vegetables, algae wafers, and occasional protein foods. They prefer warm water at 75-82°F with moderate to strong flow. Royal plecos are territorial toward other large bottom-dwellers, so provide ample space and hiding spots. They are slow-growing but eventually reach an impressive size, so plan accordingly. Strong filtration is necessary due to the large amount of wood-based waste they produce.

name: Bala Shark
description: The bala shark is a large, elegant fish from the rivers and lakes of Southeast Asia, including Thailand, Borneo, Sumatra, and the Malay Peninsula. Despite its name, it is not a true shark but a large cyprinid related to barbs and minnows, earning the shark moniker from its tall, triangular dorsal fin and torpedo-shaped body. Bala sharks are sleek, silver fish with distinctive black-edged fins that give them a striking appearance at any size. They are fast, active swimmers that can reach 14 inches in length, far exceeding the expectations of most aquarists who purchase them as small, appealing juveniles. Bala sharks are peaceful despite their size but require very large aquariums that few hobbyists can provide.
care_tips: Bala sharks need a very large aquarium of at least 150 gallons for a group, as they are active schooling fish that reach 14 inches. Keep them in groups of at least five, as solitary specimens become skittish and stressed. They are powerful jumpers that absolutely require a heavy, tight-fitting lid. Feed quality pellets, flakes, and frozen foods at 72-82°F. Despite their size, they are peaceful and can be kept with other large, non-aggressive fish. They are easily startled and may injure themselves by crashing into tank walls during panic, so place the tank in a low-traffic area. Do not purchase bala sharks unless you can commit to a very large tank for their entire lifespan of 10+ years.

name: Tinfoil Barb
description: The tinfoil barb is a large, silvery fish from the rivers and lakes of Thailand, Borneo, Sumatra, and the Malay Peninsula. Its shimmering, mirror-like silver scales reflect light brilliantly, while its red-tinged tail and dorsal fin add a flash of color. Tinfoil barbs can grow to 14 inches and are powerful, fast swimmers that need enormous amounts of space. Like bala sharks, they are frequently sold as small, attractive juveniles without adequate warning about their eventual adult size. They are schooling fish that should be kept in groups, compounding the space requirements. A school of full-grown tinfoil barbs is an impressive sight but requires a tank measured in hundreds of gallons.
care_tips: Tinfoil barbs require a very large aquarium of at least 200 gallons for a group of adults, as they reach 14 inches and are highly active schooling fish. Keep them in groups of at least five at 72-82°F. They are not suitable for standard home aquariums. Feed quality pellets, flakes, vegetables, and frozen foods. Tinfoil barbs will eat live plants, so use artificial decorations or very hardy plants. They are peaceful despite their size but their vigorous swimming and large bulk can intimidate smaller tankmates. Strong filtration is essential for the heavy bioload of a group of large fish. A very secure lid is necessary, as they can jump powerfully. Only purchase if you have adequate space for their adult size.
